news.originalContent:
Iran has openly claimed its strikes on Gulf states throughout the war. So why is it denying an attack on Kuwait?

Two Italian technicians have been killed in a drone attack on a military site in Kuwait on Thursday, the first European civilians to die amid the United States-Israel war on Iran.

Kuwait and Italy have both blamed Iran. Tehran, which has for the most part not denied, outright, strikes on US military assets hosted by its Gulf neighbours and described those attacks as self-defence, has this time denied any role and has suggested the strike was a “false-flag” operation.

The denial has raised two questions: Who was behind the attack and, if it was Iran, why is it not taking responsibility?

On Thursday, several drones targeted military installations in Kuwait, according to Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani.

Kuwait’s army initially described the target only as a “vital site”. Tajani later told the Italian Senate that it included an air-defence detection station where two technicians from Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian arm of the German defence company, were working.

The men were named by Italian media as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, from Formia, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, from Rome. They were maintaining detection antennae for the Skyguard air defence system used by Kuwait’s armed forces.

They were killed by falling shrapnel after the drones were intercepted, according to Kuwaiti and Italian reports. A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were injured.

The two dead men are the first European civilians to be killed as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran since it began in late February. A French soldier was killed in a drone attack in Iraq in March.

This was the first fatal strike on Kuwait in several months, although the country has been one of the hardest-hit Gulf states during the war. Its oil facilities, power infrastructure and airport have all been targeted at various points in the conflict. An Indian traveller was killed and 63 people were injured when drones hit Kuwait international airport on June 3 .

Iran said it last struck Kuwait on November 18 .

Both countries have blamed Iran for Thursday’s drone strike.

Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry condemned what it called a “sinful” attack and said the country reserved its right to take all measures to protect its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents.

After a call between Kuwait’s foreign minister and Tajani, the Kuwaiti ministry said the two had jointly condemned the strike.

Tajani told the Italian parliament the drones were “of Iranian origin”. The Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, Jasem Albudaiwi, also condemned what he called a “brutal attack”.

Iran has denied any involvement.

“The incident is suspicious and looks like a pre-cooked recipe for war,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X.

Araghchi called both his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts to deny Iranian involvement and offered to mount a joint investigation, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. As of Thursday evening, Kuwait had not publicly commented on the call with Araghchi.

Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi, speaking for both the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the regular army, said Iranian forces had conducted “no military or offensive operations whatsoever” in the region. He called the attack a “false flag” operation, while a military statement accused the US and Israel of using it as cover for continued aggression.

The Iranian embassy in Rome said it “categorically rejects the allegation”, suggesting the attack could have been staged to drag Europe into the Iran war.

The denial stands out because Iran has rarely disowned its attacks since US-Israeli strikes began in February. In November alone, it issued five statements claiming strikes on neighbouring states, four of them on Bahrain and Kuwait.

Tehran usually tries to justify those strikes as self-defence, arguing that it targets US bases from which Iran is attacked, not the countries that host them.

This is not the first time Iran has denied an attack on Kuwait, however. When a power and desalination plant was hit on March 30 , killing an Indian worker, Iran also claimed that Israel was responsible.

Hassan Ahmadian, a professor of Middle East studies at the University of Tehran, said Iran’s record of claiming its strikes should be taken seriously.

“Whenever the Iranians do something, they announce it,” he told Al Jazeera. “This time, as on three or four occasions during the war, they said, ‘This wasn’t us.'”

He argued that Iran would have little reason to hide this attack. “They’ve struck the Americans,” he said. “Would they be afraid to announce they’d hit Italians?”

Ahmadian said other parties in the region, such as Israel, might want to “complicate the situation” by blaming Iran, which he called “the ready-made party to blame”. He added that some in Iran also suspect Ukraine, which he argued has been trying to raise its strategic value to Washington.

As the US ran down its stock of expensive Patriot missile interceptor systems against a barrage of cheap, mass-produced Iranian Shahed drones, Ukraine offered its expertise to the US in March on how to combat the drones, which are also used by Russia.

Ahmadian said US involvement could not be ruled out either. Iran has previously told regional governments that the US was behind strikes on two sites during the war, he said.

“We’re looking at someone fishing in troubled waters. Otherwise, if it were the Iranians, they would have announced it,” he added.

Paolo von Schirach, president of the Global Policy Institute and a professor of political science at Bay Atlantic University in Washington, dismissed the idea of US involvement.

“It’s bizarre to suggest the United States would coordinate this attack on Kuwait, an ally in the Gulf, just to stir up feelings,” he said.

Von Schirach noted that Italy has refused to join the US war on Iran and does not support it. “Italy isn’t on America’s side in this conflict,” he said. “So we shouldn’t take this seriously.”

Muhanad Seloom, a senior non-resident fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said it was important to “separate Iranian-made from Iranian-launched and Iranian-ordered”.

Tajani described the drone as Iranian-built, of a type also used by Iran-backed militias. Seloom said that makes an Iraqi armed faction the leading alternative suspect. Such groups have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the war began.

He called Yemen’s Houthis “a distant second” and said Tehran’s own suspects, the US, Israel and Ukraine, “come with no evidence”.

“Only debris, radar tracks and a launch point can settle it,” he told Al Jazeera.

Iran’s “false-flag” defence is not new.

Seloom said Tehran first used it in March over strikes on Turkiye, Cyprus and Azerbaijan. However, he said that The Soufan Center, a US-based security think tank, found that it failed to convince Baku.

Claims have run the other way, too. The best known was the reported arrest of Mossad agents plotting bombings in Qatar and Saudi Arabia, which came to nothing, Seloom said, because neither of those governments stood behind it.

“Alleged often, verified never, as far as I can establish,” he said. “What this war has is deniable action. Hiding the author is common. Framing someone else has yet to be shown.”

In the case of Thursday’s attack, he said, Iran’s false-flag claim “stands without evidence so far”.

Abdullah al-Shayji, a professor of political science at Kuwait University, said Iran’s narrative “doesn’t come close to being rational or acceptable”.

“Iran bombed us eight days ago, on the 18th of this month, and didn’t deny it,” he said. He said Iran had fired 925 missiles and drones at Kuwait since the start of the war, and more projectiles at Gulf states and Jordan than at Israel. “This doesn’t fool anyone,” he said.

Al-Shayji said the denial comes down to who was killed and where. “Italian technicians were killed, and not at a US base,” he said.

That undermines Iran’s longstanding argument that it hits only US military targets, he said, an argument he believes had already collapsed because the US has now evacuated 16 bases in the region.

“The justification Iran has always used, ‘we don’t target countries, we target US military bases’, no longer exists,” he said.

Seloom offered two possible explanations. “Either it did not order it, or it cannot afford to own it,” he said.

He noted that Iran’s army openly claimed a strike on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem airbase last week. “This one hit a Kuwaiti site and killed European civilians, which risks turning Europe and the Gulf hosts against it,” he said.

Kuwaiti officials who spoke to Al Jazeera’s Kuwait bureau on condition of anonymity noted that Iran had not sought a joint investigation after earlier deadly attacks on Kuwait, including the drone strike on the airport.

Some Kuwaiti analysts said the denial appeared to be prompted by the victims’ nationality rather than the attack itself, and Al Jazeera’s bureau chief, Saad al-Saidi, said the Iranian statements had caused resentment in Kuwait.

Von Schirach linked the denial to the pressure Iran is under at home. “All the media reports say the economic situation in Iran is extremely bad,” he said, pointing to protests over the rising cost of living.

“I’m not saying the regime will fall, but it is feeling the heat of pressure from the street,” he said. “Iran is in a very difficult position.”

Not in a combat role, according to Seloom. “Europe’s reflex is pressure,” he said.

He pointed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who called for more pressure on Tehran, and to Rome, which lodged a complaint with Iran’s embassy while urging caution.

But Seloom said the deaths showed how far Europe is already involved. “The two men were maintaining a Gulf air defence system, so Europe is already in this war as a supplier, and its people are now exposed,” he said.

“Expect sanctions and more defensive support for the Gulf, not European strikes.”

The Italian deaths come at a sensitive moment. US President Donald Trump has said he will not consider returning to military action until early next year. That leaves mediators with a few weeks to find terms Washington will accept, chiefly a tangible Iranian concession on its nuclear programme.

Iran has so far stated that it will not discuss its nuclear programme until seven conditions, including the lifting of sanctions and a guaranteed end to US strikes, are met.

Seloom said the drone attack on Kuwait “narrows the track without closing it”. The indirect channel was still running on the day of the strike, he said, with proposals moving through Qatar and Pakistan, according to Araghchi’s own account.

But talks have already stalled and the public position of Qatar, one of the main mediators, is that continued attacks on Kuwait put diplomacy at risk, Seloom said.

He added that the strike strengthens the case for military force, just as the option of targeting Iran’s leadership is being discussed in Washington, according to NBC News. “Washington’s reaction matters more than Kuwait’s,” he said.

Al-Shayji said that whoever is responsible for the drone strikes on Kuwait, Iran’s attacks on Gulf states generally risk lasting damage. “Iran needs to understand that taking revenge on America this way creates enmity with a whole generation” in the Gulf, he said. He added that Kuwait is documenting every Iranian attack and will likely seek compensation.

Ahmadian said confidence building has to go both ways. “Iran didn’t start the war,” he said. “Both sides need to talk about reality, not deny it.”

news.originalTitle: Russia’s hybrid war on Europe evolving, but failing: IISS
news.title: Russia’s hybrid war on Europe evolving, but failing: IISS
news.originalSummary:

news.originalContent:
Growing sabotage and cyberattacks have damaged European infrastructure, but have not reduced support for Ukraine, analysis says.

Russia’s hybrid war on Europe continues to evolve, but has failed in its objective to deter support for Ukraine, according to analysts.

Moscow has been increasing its use of unconventional warfare in the past year or so, employing sabotage, reconnaissance and intimidation, the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a report published on Thursday.

Moscow has rejected accusations from Western governments and intelligence services that it is waging a Europe-wide campaign to disrupt support for Kyiv.

Incidents have included a drone attack on a German airport, arson and other attacks on energy infrastructure and defence manufacturers, and persistent airspace and border incursions.

Sabotage ‌attacks on European infrastructure rose by 16 percent in the 12 months leading up to September 2026, the IISS said. The use of arson and explosives roughly doubled.

“Targeting ⁠of critical infrastructure (specifically military-industrial and transport) accounted for more than half of recorded incidents between October 2025 and ⁠September 2026,” the IISS said.

The “attacks have damaged European critical infrastructure (ECI) and raised the costs of protection”, it noted.

Attacks are also becoming more sophisticated, according to the report.

“Unskilled recruits still carry out most operations. But a semi-skilled tier now uses more complex methods, including improvised explosive devices with timed and remote detonators,” the report reads.

Russian intelligence services remain a threat to European security, the IISS said, but noted that European support for Ukraine in its nearly five-year defence against Russia’s invasion has not been deterred.

“Russia’s unconventional war on Europe has so far failed in its strategic purpose,” with military assistance to Ukraine from Western allies continuing to increase, the report said.

IISS data shows that European defence spending grew by 12.6 percent in real terms in 2025, matching the rate of 2024, while Russia’s rose by 3 percent.

NATO has expanded surveillance of the Baltic Sea and its eastern airspace, while the European Union has launched a Preparedness Union Strategy.

Germany and Poland, the main conduits for military support for Ukraine, have suffered the most incidents. IISS predicts they will remain the main targets.

On Tuesday, Britain warned ⁠defence companies working with Ukraine’s military that they faced an increased sabotage threat.

Russia’s embassy in London retorted that “Russia has no plans, reasons or intentions to attack the UK.”

news.originalContent:
Redevelopment reshapes the city, but some worry as residents are displaced and cultural heritage appears at risk.

Osh, Kyrgyzstan – Kyrgyzstan’s second-largest city is in the throes of a major regeneration programme.

New IT hubs are planned for Osh, as well as apartments, schools and nurseries. Transport projects, a waste-to-energy plant and a livestock complex are being worked on too. A “modern school” for 530 children, kitted out with solar panels, was completed in 10 months and will open in the coming days, the government announced last week.

But several hundred homes have been demolished to make way for new infrastructure, stirring fears about the future and the character of the old city.

The fast-paced campaign to modernise could also affect Osh’s mountain of Sulaiman-Too – a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Osh lies just 5km from the border with Uzbekistan and is home to about 470,000 people – about 40 percent are Uzbek.

Kyrgyz authorities in the town “want to erase us from the history of this city”, said 84-year-old Mogamed Kambarow, an Uzbek with a white beard and sun-bronzed face. In March, about a third of his home was destroyed as municipal authorities worked to widen Alisher Navoi Street.

“They sent bulldozers, pulled down the walls and left,” said Kambarow, who was at home at the time. He received no compensation and lives in the remaining parts.

Neighbours alerted each other when the demolition began. An 11-year-old girl was injured by falling bricks and taken to hospital, he said.

Kambarow’s memories haunt him. He was around when violence engulfed the city before.

In 2010, inter-communal tensions spilled over into violence. More than 400 people were killed and thousands of homes were destroyed. Most of the victims were ethnic Uzbeks.

In 1990, shortly before the collapse of the Soviet Union, as Uzbeks demanded more autonomy and as land disputes raged, fighting and riots broke out between the two groups and hundreds were killed.

But Gulgaky Mamasalieva, head of the International Centre Interbilim, an organisation in Osh that provides legal help to residents today, says the current redevelopment affects everyone.

“It isn’t only Uzbek property that is damaged,” she told Al Jazeera, adding that more than 750 households were affected by the latest demolitions, including many Kyrgyz families.

According to a report by Interbilim, 65 percent of households first learned that their homes were going to be demolished when city workers painted the Russian word snos, meaning “demolition”, on their walls.

Some residents received letters telling them to leave within three days. Others, like those on Navoi Street, were visited by the mayor, who announced the plans himself.

“But people expected that there would be some paperwork done first,” said Mamasalieva.

Osh sits at the eastern end of the Ferghana Valley, the agricultural heart of Central Asia. The area is divided between three former Soviet republics: Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.

Historically, the city was predominantly Uzbek, but when the borders of the Soviet republics were drawn up in 1924-27, Moscow gave it to the Kyrgyz.

In those days, the whole city used to look like the quarters along Navoi Street, where flat-roofed houses hide behind high fences and yards full of grapevines offer some shade from the scorching sun. These areas are known as “mahallas” – an old word for an administrative and community unit.

As the years passed, a university was established, factories built, and the population grew.

Just behind Kambarow’s house, a path leads up Sulaiman-Too. The mountain is a holy site for Muslims and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009.

It is believed that the ancient Greek geographer Ptolemy mentioned the mountain in his book Geography. Babur, who was born in the Ferghana Valley and later founded the Mughal Empire, built a house of prayer on its summit.

The building was destroyed during a Soviet campaign against religion in the 1960s, but rebuilt in the late 1980s. Some Muslims believe that visiting Sulaiman-Too three times is equal to making one pilgrimage to Mecca.

There are also three cemeteries on the mountain where old gravestones rise from the long grass.

Retired pilot Abduraim Amanbaev, 73, climbs Sulaiman-Too every Friday, after prayers. He takes a shortcut through the cemetery to avoid paying the entrance fee, as the mountain is also a tourist attraction.

“The oldest grave dates back to the 14th century,” Amanbaev said.

His family home has been destroyed three times during his lifetime. The first time was in the 1960s, when the Soviet authorities modernised the city. The second was in 2010, during the ethnic violence. Now, it is happening again. “People are tired,” he said. Half of his house was destroyed. He lives in the other half and has not been compensated.

Mamasalieva from Interbilim told Al Jazeera that the city was supposed to agree on compensation with each household before demolishing their property. Disputes should have gone to court. While they received guarantee papers signed electronically by the vice-mayor, the documents did not detail compensation packages, she said.

Only families whose houses were completely destroyed were offered new flats. More than 100 households were moved to Ene-Say, a residential area 10km (6 miles) outside Osh. Another 64 families were given flats in an apartment block in the city.

But for some, relocation has caused further problems.

“We still haven’t been given the deeds for this flat,” said a 37-year-old woman who now lives in Ene-Say, who requested anonymity.

Without official ownership, her family cannot register their new address or access free healthcare and other services. Some families said they have also been asked to pay the government the difference between the value of their old homes and their new flats.

Interbilim said it is ready to help residents take the authorities to court, but so far nobody has been willing to do so.

“The city promised that anyone who wanted to open a business along Navoi Street would be given permission,” said Mamasalieva.

Osh’s debts total up to 3 billion soms ($34m), according to Kyrgyz media. City authorities rejected that figure when contacted by Al Jazeera, saying the budget for this year is 5.2 billion soms ($57m). Officials did not respond to questions regarding the backlash over the development plans.

Sulaiman-Too is a key source of tourism income. It attracts about 370,000 visitors each year, according to Hairullo Ibaydullaev, a deputy director of the National Historical and Archaeological Museum Complex Sulayman, which is carved inside the mountain.

Renovation across the mountain began in October. The plans include improving the footpaths, replacing lighting and building a car park. The $12m project is being funded by the World Bank and is expected to take one year.

But Ibaydullaev said the mountain is under pressure from developers who want to use the surrounding land, even though it is protected by UNESCO. The mountain has a buffer zone covering 4,788 hectares (11,830 acres), which includes Navoi Street.

City officials say these restrictions make it harder to develop Osh.

Sabira Soltongeldieva, head of the National Commission of the Kyrgyz Republic for UNESCO, said that Bishkek has asked to reconsider how the buffer zone is used.

The former mayor, Jenishbek Toktorboev, asked the Ministry of Culture to release some of the protected land for new projects. He earned the nickname “Demolition Uncle” among some after he ordered the destruction of the old Jayma Bazaar, once the city’s main trading centres.

“The vendors were given 15 days to disappear,” said a knife-maker, whose stall was one of those allowed to remain.

Toktorboev also began building apartment blocks at the foot of the mountain, taller than the rules for the buffer zone allowed. He wanted to remove one of the three cemeteries and build a leisure park in its place. This project failed. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov dismissed him in February.

The new mayor, Janar Akaev, has continued to propose new developments.

In August, Akaev announced plans to build a cable car to the top of the mountain, comparing it to those in Switzerland.

He also announced a plan to remove the mountain from the UNESCO World Heritage list – a proposal rejected by the culture ministry.

“This is the most complete example of a sacred mountain in Central Asia,” said Ibaydullaev.

news.originalContent:
The vote could reshape diplomatic relations, but shared strategic interests will continue to bind the two countries.

Professor of international relations at Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University in Fez, Morocco.

Spain’s November 29 general election comes at a difficult moment both domestically and internationally. The snap election was triggered by an internal political crisis after parliament voted down the government’s housing decrees including stronger protections for tenants, with one of the ruling coalition’s members going against the proposals.

Foreign policy crises have also cast a shadow over the election, significantly influencing the substance of the campaign and potentially its outcome. Of particular importance are Spain’s relations with Morocco, which involve several sensitive and overlapping issues, notably the status of Ceuta and Melilla, irregular migration and the question of Western Sahara. These have placed Morocco at the heart of Spain’s political and electoral debate in recent months.

A poll conducted by Cluster17 showed that relations with Morocco and the situation in Ceuta and Melilla topped the list of international issues likely to influence how Spaniards vote, with 34 percent of respondents selecting them. Relations with the United States came a distant second at 9 percent, followed by the conflict in the Middle East at 8 percent and the war in Ukraine at 4 percent.

The positions Spanish political parties have adopted towards Morocco during the election campaign range from moderate to confrontational. While incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who remains in office until the election, has taken a restrained and cautious approach towards Morocco, parties such as Vox have adopted a more hardline stance, going so far as to promise a review of Spain’s relations with its southern neighbour.

A distinction must be drawn, however, between the electoral promises parties make in the media, sometimes in an attempt to outbid their political rivals and how they actually exercise power.

Political parties may adopt more hardline positions while in opposition or on the campaign trail, but once in government, they become responsible for managing the affairs of the state, rather than merely pursuing their party agendas.

This often prompts them to adopt more pragmatic approaches, particularly on foreign policy issues of strategic importance. Moreover, on certain issues, such as Western Sahara, existing state commitments limit the parties’ room for manoeuvre and require a degree of caution. Regional and international balances of power also remain important factors in shaping foreign policy.

To understand Spain’s political and electoral debate over Morocco and its implications for relations between the two countries, it is necessary to distinguish between three categories of issues on which their interests intersect and sometimes conflict: immediate concerns, medium-term interests and long-term strategic issues.

This distinction helps separate crises arising from short-term political developments from structural disagreements that transcend changes in government and the balance of power between political parties.

The first category encompasses immediate issues and short-term political tensions. These are closely intertwined with Spain’s domestic political landscape, both shaping and being shaped by the balance of power within parliament and government. The 2002 crisis over Perejil Island and the migration crisis in Ceuta in the summer of 2026 offer two contrasting examples.

The former occurred under the Popular Party government led by Jose Maria Aznar and developed into a political and military confrontation. Relations gradually returned to normal following an agreement to restore the status quo, brokered by then-US Secretary of State Colin Powell.

The 2026 crisis, meanwhile, occurred under a left-wing coalition government, which largely succeeded in containing it. Although the episode was described in Spain as the most tragic mass border crossing in the country’s history, with some 72,000 migrants crossing the border in a single week, the government was able to manage the crisis but could not escape its domestic political repercussions.

From this perspective, some of the current electoral rhetoric towards Morocco can be understood as a reflection of domestic political competition rather than a new strategic direction. Hardline positions on Ceuta and Melilla, migration and relations with Rabat should be viewed in the context of the competition for votes, bearing in mind the distinction between electoral promises and the feasibility of translating them into government policy.

The second category concerns the shared economic, security and political interests that form the backbone of Moroccan-Spanish relations. These include trade and investment, cooperation on energy, migration and border control, and efforts to combat terrorism and organised crime.

The importance of this category lies in the practical and immediate nature of these interests, which would be difficult for any Spanish government, regardless of its political affiliation, to ignore or sacrifice.

Although these interests are sometimes affected by short-term political tensions, they require both countries to exercise a degree of pragmatism and caution in managing their differences. They are therefore among the most important factors in containing crises and ensuring the continuity of bilateral cooperation.

The third category encompasses long-term strategic and structural issues dictated by geography and history, which are not necessarily determined by the political orientation of successive governments.

Foremost among these are the status of Ceuta and Melilla and the other islands Morocco seeks to reclaim and the question of Western Sahara. They also include the countries’ perceptions of one another, shaped by history, collective memory and political discourse, which have influenced how each views the other and understands its own place and role in the region.

These issues differ from immediate disputes in that they are rooted in strategic considerations and longstanding political and historical claims. Despite their prominence in the current political and electoral debate, their use in party rhetoric remains largely driven by short-term electoral considerations and does not necessarily reflect a coherent state strategy. Their significance extends beyond Spain’s partisan disagreements.

Against this backdrop, the prominence of certain Morocco-related issues in Spain’s political and electoral contest can be understood primarily in terms of immediate concerns and short-term political tensions.

The outcome of the Spanish election may therefore affect how these issues are managed and the level of political trust between the two countries, but it will not necessarily alter the foundations of their relationship. Shared interests necessitate continued cooperation, while major strategic issues remain contingent on deeper, longer-term changes.

The upcoming Spanish election leaves Morocco facing uncertainty over the nature of the political partner Rabat will be dealing with in the coming years. Three main scenarios for the future of bilateral relations can be envisaged, depending on the composition of the next government and the balance of power between the parties that will shape its foreign policy.

The first scenario is that the Socialist Party remains in power, despite the difficulties it faces and the possibility of an electoral defeat. Should this scenario materialise, a victory for Sanchez would likely preserve the road map launched in April 2022 and sustain the rapprochement that followed Spain’s shift in position on Western Sahara.

Economic and security cooperation, as well as cooperation on migration management, would also be expected to continue. At the same time, Sanchez would seek to strengthen energy relations with Algeria. It is worth noting that Algeria supplied about 34 percent of Spain’s natural gas imports in the first half of 2026, overtaking the US.

The second scenario involves the Popular Party coming to power. This could open the door to a review of certain aspects of Spanish foreign policy, particularly the balance Spain seeks to maintain in its relations with its North African neighbours.

This would not necessarily mean a weakening of the partnership with Rabat, however, as Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo may adopt a more pragmatic approach than his party’s electoral positions suggest. His stance on Morocco’s autonomy initiative for Western Sahara, along with the nature of his relationship with Vox, would be among the key factors shaping this scenario.

The third scenario involves Vox joining the government or the government relying on its parliamentary support. This could lead to an escalation in hardline rhetoric on Ceuta and Melilla and migration, and possibly to calls for a review of agreements and relations with Morocco. This could undermine political trust and bilateral cooperation, particularly if Vox imposes conditions on the Popular Party.

There could also be a hardening of rhetoric and policies on migration, alongside symbolic acts of escalation, such as threatening to withdraw from cohosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup or provoking a dispute over which country will host the final.

There were already signs of both following the Ceuta crisis. The Popular Party rejected the prospect of cohosting the World Cup unless the final was held in Spain, making the country’s participation conditional on this demand. Vox, meanwhile, submitted a non-legislative motion calling on the government to urge FIFA to exclude Morocco from hosting the tournament and to ensure that Spain hosts the final.

Nevertheless, Vox’s ability to translate its positions into policy would remain constrained by coalition dynamics, European commitments and shared economic and security interests.

Ultimately, regardless of the outcome, the election will present a new test of Rabat and Madrid’s ability to separate short-term political tensions from their shared strategic interests.

While the results may affect the level of political trust and the way contentious issues are managed, mutual geopolitical, economic and security interests will remain fundamental to ensuring the continuity of cooperation.

It is also in Morocco’s interest to maintain channels of communication with the various Spanish political forces, including the current opposition parties, in anticipation of changes in government and political orientation. At the same time, Morocco should continue to pursue a strategy of hedging and diversifying its partnerships to increase its diplomatic room for manoeuvre.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

While incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who remains in office until the election, has taken a restrained and cautious approach towards Morocco, parties such as Vox have adopted a more hardline stance, going so far as to promise a review of Spain’s relations with its southern neighbour.

A distinction must be drawn, however, between the electoral promises parties make in the media, sometimes in an attempt to outbid their political rivals and how they actually exercise power.

Political parties may adopt more hardline positions while in opposition or on the campaign trail, but once in government, they become responsible for managing the affairs of the state, rather than merely pursuing their party agendas.

This often prompts them to adopt more pragmatic approaches, particularly on foreign policy issues of strategic importance. Moreover, on certain issues, such as Western Sahara, existing state commitments limit the parties’ room for manoeuvre and require a degree of caution. Regional and international balances of power also remain important factors in shaping foreign policy.

To understand Spain’s political and electoral debate over Morocco and its implications for relations between the two countries, it is necessary to distinguish between three categories of issues on which their interests intersect and sometimes conflict: immediate concerns, medium-term interests and long-term strategic issues.

This distinction helps separate crises arising from short-term political developments from structural disagreements that transcend changes in government and the balance of power between political parties.

The first category encompasses immediate issues and short-term political tensions. These are closely intertwined with Spain’s domestic political landscape, both shaping and being shaped by the balance of power within parliament and government. The 2002 crisis over Perejil Island and the migration crisis in Ceuta in the summer of 2026 offer two contrasting examples.

The former occurred under the Popular Party government led by Jose Maria Aznar and developed into a political and military confrontation. Relations gradually returned to normal following an agreement to restore the status quo, brokered by then-US Secretary of State Colin Powell.

The 2026 crisis, meanwhile, occurred under a left-wing coalition government, which largely succeeded in containing it. Although the episode was described in Spain as the most tragic mass border crossing in the country’s history, with some 72,000 migrants crossing the border in a single week, the government was able to manage the crisis but could not escape its domestic political repercussions.

From this perspective, some of the current electoral rhetoric towards Morocco can be understood as a reflection of domestic political competition rather than a new strategic direction. Hardline positions on Ceuta and Melilla, migration and relations with Rabat should be viewed in the context of the competition for votes, bearing in mind the distinction between electoral promises and the feasibility of translating them into government policy.

The second category concerns the shared economic, security and political interests that form the backbone of Moroccan-Spanish relations. These include trade and investment, cooperation on energy, migration and border control, and efforts to combat terrorism and organised crime.

The importance of this category lies in the practical and immediate nature of these interests, which would be difficult for any Spanish government, regardless of its political affiliation, to ignore or sacrifice.

Although these interests are sometimes affected by short-term political tensions, they require both countries to exercise a degree of pragmatism and caution in managing their differences. They are therefore among the most important factors in containing crises and ensuring the continuity of bilateral cooperation.

The third category encompasses long-term strategic and structural issues dictated by geography and history, which are not necessarily determined by the political orientation of successive governments.

Foremost among these are the status of Ceuta and Melilla and the other islands Morocco seeks to reclaim and the question of Western Sahara. They also include the countries’ perceptions of one another, shaped by history, collective memory and political discourse, which have influenced how each views the other and understands its own place and role in the region.

These issues differ from immediate disputes in that they are rooted in strategic considerations and longstanding political and historical claims. Despite their prominence in the current political and electoral debate, their use in party rhetoric remains largely driven by short-term electoral considerations and does not necessarily reflect a coherent state strategy. Their significance extends beyond Spain’s partisan disagreements.

Against this backdrop, the prominence of certain Morocco-related issues in Spain’s political and electoral contest can be understood primarily in terms of immediate concerns and short-term political tensions.

The outcome of the Spanish election may therefore affect how these issues are managed and the level of political trust between the two countries, but it will not necessarily alter the foundations of their relationship. Shared interests necessitate continued cooperation, while major strategic issues remain contingent on deeper, longer-term changes.

The upcoming Spanish election leaves Morocco facing uncertainty over the nature of the political partner Rabat will be dealing with in the coming years. Three main scenarios for the future of bilateral relations can be envisaged, depending on the composition of the next government and the balance of power between the parties that will shape its foreign policy.

The first scenario is that the Socialist Party remains in power, despite the difficulties it faces and the possibility of an electoral defeat. Should this scenario materialise, a victory for Sanchez would likely preserve the road map launched in April 2022 and sustain the rapprochement that followed Spain’s shift in position on Western Sahara.

Economic and security cooperation, as well as cooperation on migration management, would also be expected to continue. At the same time, Sanchez would seek to strengthen energy relations with Algeria. It is worth noting that Algeria supplied about 34 percent of Spain’s natural gas imports in the first half of 2026, overtaking the US.

The second scenario involves the Popular Party coming to power. This could open the door to a review of certain aspects of Spanish foreign policy, particularly the balance Spain seeks to maintain in its relations with its North African neighbours.

This would not necessarily mean a weakening of the partnership with Rabat, however, as Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo may adopt a more pragmatic approach than his party’s electoral positions suggest. His stance on Morocco’s autonomy initiative for Western Sahara, along with the nature of his relationship with Vox, would be among the key factors shaping this scenario.

The third scenario involves Vox joining the government or the government relying on its parliamentary support. This could lead to an escalation in hardline rhetoric on Ceuta and Melilla and migration, and possibly to calls for a review of agreements and relations with Morocco. This could undermine political trust and bilateral cooperation, particularly if Vox imposes conditions on the Popular Party.

There could also be a hardening of rhetoric and policies on migration, alongside symbolic acts of escalation, such as threatening to withdraw from cohosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup or provoking a dispute over which country will host the final.

There were already signs of both following the Ceuta crisis. The Popular Party rejected the prospect of cohosting the World Cup unless the final was held in Spain, making the country’s participation conditional on this demand. Vox, meanwhile, submitted a non-legislative motion calling on the government to urge FIFA to exclude Morocco from hosting the tournament and to ensure that Spain hosts the final.

Nevertheless, Vox’s ability to translate its positions into policy would remain constrained by coalition dynamics, European commitments and shared economic and security interests.

Ultimately, regardless of the outcome, the election will present a new test of Rabat and Madrid’s ability to separate short-term political tensions from their shared strategic interests.

While the results may affect the level of political trust and the way contentious issues are managed, mutual geopolitical, economic and security interests will remain fundamental to ensuring the continuity of cooperation.

It is also in Morocco’s interest to maintain channels of communication with the various Spanish political forces, including the current opposition parties, in anticipation of changes in government and political orientation. At the same time, Morocco should continue to pursue a strategy of hedging and diversifying its partnerships to increase its diplomatic room for manoeuvre.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

news.originalContent:
Israel seeking ‘to prevent births’ and destroy Palestinians in Gaza by targeting women and girls, rights group says.

Israel has sought “to prevent births” in Gaza by repeatedly targeting women and girls, according to Amnesty International.

The rights group said in a report that Israeli forces have killed about 30 women and girls daily since October 2023, while Israel’s blockade on the Strip has led to an untold number of additional female deaths.

The killings, forced displacement, starvation and disruption of critical healthcare services are part of a deliberate drive to prevent the growth of the Palestinian population, the report said – a strategy recognised as constituting genocide.

“Over the past three years, Israel has demonstrated an unending calculated intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza,”  Agnes CallamardAgnes Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International, said.

“Women and girls in Gaza have endured a relentless assault on every aspect of their lives. They have been killed, injured, displaced, starved and denied access to essential healthcare, while systematically stripped of the conditions necessary to make decisions about pregnancy, childbirth and their reproductive futures,” Callamard added.

The report cites harrowing accounts of female survivors who were forced to endure difficult premature births and faced attacks as Israeli forces targeted hospitals caring for incubated babies. Others said they suffered life-altering injuries in attacks, as well as miscarriages and stillbirths.

Israel’s attacks and restrictions have decimated medical infrastructure, cut off access to maternal healthcare, and hampered the flow of medicines and other essential medical needs, the rights group noted.

All nine fertilisation clinics in the enclave have been destroyed, along with eggs and embryos, the report said. Repeated forced displacement orders have further exposed women to gender-based violence.

Preventing births and the intent to destroy life within a group constitute genocide, according to the United Nations’ Genocide Convention.

Amnesty International declared that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza in 2024. Targeting women, girls and reproductive health services was an “integral” part of Israel’s campaign, the group said in its latest report.

Callamard called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to examine gender-based crimes as part of its ongoing investigation into Israel’s alleged war crimes.

Israel has killed close to 75,000 people in Gaza, according to data from Gaza’s Health Ministry. At least 22,331 women and girls were killed between October 7, 2023 and October 1, 2026, the report said.

news.originalContent:
Paris Fury had claimed mental health diagnosis for Tyson Fury following his victory over Ukraine’s Wladimir Klitschko.

Paris Fury, the wife of Tyson Fury, has retracted her claim that the British heavyweight was diagnosed with schizophrenia just months after he was crowned world champion in 2015.

In clips promoting a Netflix documentary, the boxer spoke about his mental health struggles following his victory over Ukraine’s Wladimir Klitschko in Germany.

Paris Fury said Tyson Fury had “mild schizophrenia” in an initial version of the documentary, which will be released on Friday.

Netflix said it had worked to “update” the footage in light of her clarification.

Fury, 38, is due to face Anthony Joshua in a long-awaited all-British showdown in Cardiff on December 11.

Paris Fury’s comments come after the British Boxing Board of Control indicated that it was investigating the earlier comments, though Robert Smith, the board’s general secretary, told the BBC it was “fairly confident” he would be cleared to fight Joshua.

“I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary,” Paris said in a statement.

“I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word ‘schizophrenic’. Whilst Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.

“Mental health is complex, and it isn’t always easy to find the right words, especially when you’re living it with someone you love.

“I’m so proud of Tyson for really opening up in this documentary and want to say thank you for all the support we’ve received as a family.”

Fury has been open about his mental health struggles since beating Klitschko, after which he took a break of nearly three years from boxing.

His weight ballooned while he battled suicidal thoughts and drug and alcohol problems.

Fury admitted hearing “voices in my mind” following his win, adding: “Words can’t explain the darkness I was in.

“I came from the living version of the pits of hellfire. And I 100 percent thought at times I’d end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.”

Fury became world heavyweight champion for a second time when he beat WBC champion Deontay Wilder in February 2020.

Despite losing twice to Oleksandr Usyk in 2024, the only losses in his 39-fight professional career, Fury could become a three-time world champion when he takes on Joshua with the vacant WBA title set to be on the line.

Netflix said in a statement: “Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch.”

news.originalContent:
نخستین تصاویر از سیارکی که یک فضاپیما عمدا با آن برخورد کرده بود، دهانه‌ای به اندازه یک ورزشگاه را روی سطح آن نشان می‌دهد.

این خسارت گسترده زمانی ایجاد شد که در سال ۲۰۲۲، یک فضاپیمای ناسا عمدا به سیارک دیمورفوس برخورد کرد. این سیارک هیچ تهدیدی برای زمین محسوب نمی‌شد، اما هدف از این آزمایش، ارزیابی توانایی دفاع سیاره‌ای و بررسی این موضوع بود که آیا می‌توان یک جرم سنگی فضایی را از مسیر خود منحرف کرد یا نه.

اکنون، چهار سال بعد، فضاپیمایی به نام «هرا» متعلق به آژانس فضایی اروپا، در حال بررسی دقیق محل برخورد است تا پیامدهای آن را به‌طور کامل ارزیابی کند.

دکتر سابینا رادوکان، دانشمند علوم سیاره‌ای و عضو گروه علمی ماموریت هرا، گفت: «این دهانه تقریبا به اندازه خود سیارک است و واقعا منظره‌ای شگفت‌انگیز دارد.»

او افزود: «توصیف این همه هیجان با کلمات دشوار است، اینکه بالاخره بتوانیم ببینیم چه اتفاقی افتاده است. به‌عنوان کسی که در زمینه دهانه‌های برخوردی تحقیق می‌کند، می‌توانم بگویم که زیبا هم هست.»

آزمایش اولیه برخورد در سال ۲۰۲۲ با فضاپیمای ناسا به نام «دارت» انجام شد که با سرعت ۲۲ هزار کیلومتر در ساعت به دیمورفوس برخورد کرد.

شدت برخورد به اندازه‌ای بود که دنباله‌ای از آوار و ذرات پراکنده به طول حدود ۱۰ هزار کیلومتر ایجاد شد که تلسکوپ‌های زمینی و فضایی توانستند آن را مشاهده کنند.

دیمورفوس حدود ۱۵۰ متر پهنا دارد. یکی از دلایل انتخاب آن به‌عنوان هدف این بود که بخشی از یک منظومه دوتایی سیارکی است و به دور جرم سنگی بزرگ‌تری به نام دیدیموس می‌چرخد که حدود ۷۳۰ متر پهنا دارد.

این برخورد نشان داد که تغییر مسیر سیارک کوچک‌تر امکان‌پذیر است.

پیش از برخورد، دیمورفوس هر ۱۱ ساعت و ۵۵ دقیقه یکبار به دور دیدیموس می‌چرخید. پس از برخورد، مدت گردش مداری آن حدود ۳۳ دقیقه کاهش یافت.

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

رسیدن فضاپیمای هرا به محل برخورد اکنون به دانشمندان کمک می‌کند به پرسش‌های بسیار بیشتری پاسخ دهند.

این برخورد نه تنها شکل دیمورفوس را تغییر داد، بلکه نحوه حرکت آن را نیز دگرگون کرد.

رادوکان توضیح داد: «پیش از برخورد دارت، دیمورفوس بیشتر شبیه ماه خودمان بود یعنی همیشه یک سمت آن رو به دیدیموس قرار داشت و حرکت بسیار منظمی داشت.»

او افزود: «اما اکنون حرکتش بسیار نامنظم شده و مدام غلت می‌خورد. تصور کنید بشکه‌ای را از پله‌ها به پایین می‌اندازید و بشکه در حال غلتیدن و حرکت است. اساسا دیمورفوس اکنون به همین شکل به دور دیدیموس حرکت می‌کند.»

هرا همچنین تصاویر دقیقی از دیدیموس گرفته که جزئیات سطح آن را آشکار کرده‌اند.

نائومی مرداک، از اعضای گروه ماموریت هرا، گفت: «گرانش در سطح دیدیموس حدود یک چهل‌ هزارم گرانش زمین است.»

او افزود: «همین حالا می‌توانیم ساختارهای زمین‌شناختی جذاب و پیچیده‌ای را ببینیم. مناطقی را می‌بینیم که پوشیده از تخته‌ سنگ هستند.»

«کوچک‌ترین عوارضی که می‌توانیم در این تصاویر تشخیص دهیم، حدود سه متر اندازه دارند. این یعنی تمام تخته‌ سنگ‌هایی که با چشم می‌بینید دست‌کم سه متر و برخی حتی تا ۱۰ متر اندازه دارند. بنابراین آنچه در اینجا می‌بینیم، تخته‌ سنگ‌هایی به اندازه خودروها و اتوبوس‌ها هستند که روی جرمی آسمانی با گرانشی تقریبا ناچیز قرار گرفته‌اند.»

منبع تصویر، NASA/Hubble Space Telescope

ماموریت هرا در شش ماه آینده به مطالعه دیمورفوس و دیدیموس خواهد پرداخت و تصاویر بیشتری از فاصله نزدیک‌تر و با وضوح بالاتر به زمین خواهد فرستاد.

پاتریک میشل، پژوهشگر اصلی ماموریت هرا در آژانس فضایی اروپا، گفت: «هرا به نوعی شبیه کارآگاه کلمبو است که به صحنه برخورد بازمی‌گردد تا پیامدهای آن را بررسی کند.»

این فضاپیما به مجموعه گسترده‌ای از ابزارهای علمی مجهز است و دو ماهواره کوچک به اندازه جعبه کفش نیز حمل می‌کند که می‌توانند محل برخورد را از نزدیک بررسی کنند و سپس روی سیارک فرود بیایند.

اما نخستین تصاویر ثبت‌شده به وسیله هرا چالش تازه‌ای را نیز آشکار کرده‌اند. دیمورفوس و دیدیموس در حالی در فضا حرکت می‌کنند که صدها تخته‌ سنگ با اندازه‌هایی از چند ده سانتی‌متر تا حدود یک متر آن‌ها را احاطه کرده‌اند.

هدایت فضاپیما و ماهواره‌های مکعبی کوچک آن در میان این میدان تخته‌سنگ‌ها به‌ویژه دشوار خواهد بود.

یکی از وظایف اصلی این ماموریت اندازه‌گیری جرم دیمورفوس است تا مشخص شود ضربه فضاپیما تا چه اندازه در تغییر مسیر آن موثر بوده است.

اگر روزی جرم سنگی فضایی را شناسایی کنیم که در مسیر برخورد با زمین قرار دارد، این اطلاعات اهمیتی حیاتی خواهند داشت.

پروفسور سایمون گرین، دانشمند علوم سیاره‌ای و عضو گروه علمی هرا، گفت: «این اطلاعات به ما کمک می‌کند پیش‌بینی کنیم اگر مجبور شویم به سیارک دیگری ضربه بزنیم، چه اتفاقی خواهد افتاد.»

او افزود: «می‌توانیم ویژگی‌های آن را اندازه‌گیری کنیم و بگوییم برای اینکه مسیرش به اندازه کافی تغییر کند و از کنار زمین بگذرد، به فضاپیمایی با این میزان جرم نیاز داریم که با این سرعت و تا این اندازه زودتر به آن برخورد کند.»

سیارک‌ها تهدید قابل توجهی برای سیاره ما محسوب می‌شوند.

بزرگ‌ترین سیارک‌ها که بیش از یک کیلومتر پهنا دارند، می‌توانند ویرانی در مقیاس جهانی به بار آورند. اما حتی سیارک‌های متوسط، با ابعادی مشابه دیمورفوس، نیز می‌توانند یک شهر را به‌طور کامل نابود کنند.

کارولین ارنست از آزمایشگاه فیزیک کاربردی دانشگاه جانز هاپکینز که در هر دو ماموریت دارت و هرا مشارکت داشته، گفت: «همه ما می‌دانیم چه بر سر دایناسورها آمد، درست است؟ و نمی‌خواهیم همان اتفاق برای ما هم رخ دهد.»

او افزود: «خبر خوب برای ما این است که شمار تهدیدهای احتمالی موجود در منظومه شمسی بسیار کمتر از میلیون‌ها سال پیش است. اما هنوز اجرامی در آنجا وجود دارند.»

به گفته او، بزرگ‌ترین سیارک‌ها شناسایی شده‌اند و هیچ‌ یک در مسیر برخورد با زمین قرار ندارند.

او افزود: «کوچک‌ترین اجرام نیز تهدید چندان بزرگی نیستند، زیرا جو زمین از ما محافظت می‌کند.»

«اما در محدوده‌ای از اندازه‌های متوسط، هنوز نمی‌دانیم همه این اجرام کجا هستند و برخورد آن‌ها می‌تواند برای بشریت مشکلاتی ایجاد کند. اگر بتوانیم آن‌ها را شناسایی کنیم و درباره‌شان اطلاعات به دست آوریم، قطعا می‌خواهیم برای جلوگیری از چنین برخوردی تلاش کنیم.»

دانشمندان می‌خواهند تا حد امکان اطلاعات بیشتری درباره اجرام سنگی فضایی جمع‌آوری کنند تا انسان بتواند با هر تهدیدی که کیهان پیش روی او قرار می‌دهد، با آمادگی بیشتری مقابله کند.

در سال ۲۰۲۷ ماموریت تازه‌ای برای ردیابی سیارک‌های بالقوه خطرناک آغاز خواهد شد، این کار قرار است با تلسکوپی فضایی به نام «پویشگر اجرام نزدیک به زمین» انجام گیرد.

ماموریت‌های دیگری نیز برای بازدید از سیارک‌ها برنامه‌ریزی شده‌اند، از جمله سفر به سیارکی به نام «آپوفیس» که حدود ۴۵۰ متر طول دارد.

آپوفیس در سال ۲۰۰۴ کشف شد و در ابتدا تصور می‌شد ممکن است حتی در ۱۳ آوریل ۲۰۲۹ با زمین برخورد کند.

اما اکنون دانشمندان شناخت دقیق‌تری از مدار آن دارند و می‌گویند این سیارک دست‌کم در ۱۰۰ سال آینده با زمین برخورد نخواهد کرد. آپوفیس به‌جای برخورد با زمین در سال ۲۰۲۹، از فاصله تنها ۳۲ هزار کیلومتری سطح سیاره ما عبور خواهد کرد.

این رویداد فرصتی کم‌نظیر برای دانشمندان فراهم می‌کند تا یک جرم سنگی فضایی را از نزدیک مطالعه کنند.

دو فضاپیما به سوی آپوفیس خواهند رفت، یکی «اوسیریس اپکس» متعلق به ناسا که پیش‌تر از سیارک دیگری به نام «بنو» نمونه‌برداری کرده بود و دیگری «رامسس»، ماموریت مشترک آژانس فضایی اروپا و آژانس اکتشافات هوافضای ژاپن.

نخستین تصاویر از سیارکی که یک فضاپیما عمدا با آن برخورد کرده بود، دهانه‌ای به اندازه یک ورزشگاه را روی سطح آن نشان می‌دهد.

این خسارت گسترده زمانی ایجاد شد که در سال ۲۰۲۲، یک فضاپیمای ناسا عمدا به سیارک دیمورفوس برخورد کرد. این سیارک هیچ تهدیدی برای زمین محسوب نمی‌شد، اما هدف از این آزمایش، ارزیابی توانایی دفاع سیاره‌ای و بررسی این موضوع بود که آیا می‌توان یک جرم سنگی فضایی را از مسیر خود منحرف کرد یا نه.

اکنون، چهار سال بعد، فضاپیمایی به نام «هرا» متعلق به آژانس فضایی اروپا، در حال بررسی دقیق محل برخورد است تا پیامدهای آن را به‌طور کامل ارزیابی کند.

دکتر سابینا رادوکان، دانشمند علوم سیاره‌ای و عضو گروه علمی ماموریت هرا، گفت: «این دهانه تقریبا به اندازه خود سیارک است و واقعا منظره‌ای شگفت‌انگیز دارد.»

او افزود: «توصیف این همه هیجان با کلمات دشوار است، اینکه بالاخره بتوانیم ببینیم چه اتفاقی افتاده است. به‌عنوان کسی که در زمینه دهانه‌های برخوردی تحقیق می‌کند، می‌توانم بگویم که زیبا هم هست.»

آزمایش اولیه برخورد در سال ۲۰۲۲ با فضاپیمای ناسا به نام «دارت» انجام شد که با سرعت ۲۲ هزار کیلومتر در ساعت به دیمورفوس برخورد کرد.

شدت برخورد به اندازه‌ای بود که دنباله‌ای از آوار و ذرات پراکنده به طول حدود ۱۰ هزار کیلومتر ایجاد شد که تلسکوپ‌های زمینی و فضایی توانستند آن را مشاهده کنند.

دیمورفوس حدود ۱۵۰ متر پهنا دارد. یکی از دلایل انتخاب آن به‌عنوان هدف این بود که بخشی از یک منظومه دوتایی سیارکی است و به دور جرم سنگی بزرگ‌تری به نام دیدیموس می‌چرخد که حدود ۷۳۰ متر پهنا دارد.

این برخورد نشان داد که تغییر مسیر سیارک کوچک‌تر امکان‌پذیر است.

پیش از برخورد، دیمورفوس هر ۱۱ ساعت و ۵۵ دقیقه یکبار به دور دیدیموس می‌چرخید. پس از برخورد، مدت گردش مداری آن حدود ۳۳ دقیقه کاهش یافت.

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

رسیدن فضاپیمای هرا به محل برخورد اکنون به دانشمندان کمک می‌کند به پرسش‌های بسیار بیشتری پاسخ دهند.

این برخورد نه تنها شکل دیمورفوس را تغییر داد، بلکه نحوه حرکت آن را نیز دگرگون کرد.

رادوکان توضیح داد: «پیش از برخورد دارت، دیمورفوس بیشتر شبیه ماه خودمان بود یعنی همیشه یک سمت آن رو به دیدیموس قرار داشت و حرکت بسیار منظمی داشت.»

او افزود: «اما اکنون حرکتش بسیار نامنظم شده و مدام غلت می‌خورد. تصور کنید بشکه‌ای را از پله‌ها به پایین می‌اندازید و بشکه در حال غلتیدن و حرکت است. اساسا دیمورفوس اکنون به همین شکل به دور دیدیموس حرکت می‌کند.»

هرا همچنین تصاویر دقیقی از دیدیموس گرفته که جزئیات سطح آن را آشکار کرده‌اند.

نائومی مرداک، از اعضای گروه ماموریت هرا، گفت: «گرانش در سطح دیدیموس حدود یک چهل‌ هزارم گرانش زمین است.»

او افزود: «همین حالا می‌توانیم ساختارهای زمین‌شناختی جذاب و پیچیده‌ای را ببینیم. مناطقی را می‌بینیم که پوشیده از تخته‌ سنگ هستند.»

«کوچک‌ترین عوارضی که می‌توانیم در این تصاویر تشخیص دهیم، حدود سه متر اندازه دارند. این یعنی تمام تخته‌ سنگ‌هایی که با چشم می‌بینید دست‌کم سه متر و برخی حتی تا ۱۰ متر اندازه دارند. بنابراین آنچه در اینجا می‌بینیم، تخته‌ سنگ‌هایی به اندازه خودروها و اتوبوس‌ها هستند که روی جرمی آسمانی با گرانشی تقریبا ناچیز قرار گرفته‌اند.»

منبع تصویر، NASA/Hubble Space Telescope

news.originalContent:
Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images

Tech giants are struggling to contain their artificial intelligence agents as their bots keep finding ways to seek out users’ sensitive data.

AI agents keep trying to access private data without permission: Meta’s Muse read employee’s Signal messages and was among multiple agents screenshotting private messages, xAI’s Grokbot made several attempts to access users’ company accounts, and Google’s Gemini agents were used in an unsanctioned attempt to hack a nonprofit. These incidents are the latest in a string of incidents where AI agents took actions beyond user control, such as hacking companies and breaching private websites.

California is one of a dozen states suing OpenAI over the company’s alleged lack of safety measures.

The state demands that OpenAI pay civil penalties for damages its models have caused, referencing the July incident in which the company’s models hacked New York-based startup Hugging Face, according to California’s Nov. 17 complaint. (RELATED: Watchdogs Haul Five Tech Giants To Court Over Concerns AI Could ‘Exterminate’ Humanity)

“OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested highly cyber-capable AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public,” the California Department of Justice told the Daily Caller News Foundation. “Without proper safeguards and monitoring, these models pose a danger to anything connected to the internet.”

OpenAI did not immediately respond to the DCNF’s request for comment.

Signal, an encrypted messaging app, announced it blocked screenshots from its platform Monday, to attempt to restrict built-in mobile AI agents’ ability to extract private message data.

“Our remedy is also incomplete — while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem,” Meredith Whittaker, the president of Signal, said in a Friday company blog post.

More than 24 Meta posts reported Muse’s unprompted actions, according to Reuters’ review of the company’s internal posts about the agent.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” a Meta employee told colleagues, Reuters reported. The employee realized Muse had reminded them to respond to a private Signal message.

Muse’s access to private Signal messages and unprompted behaviors are “isolated incidents,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reuters. He also said hallucinations were the cause of several concerning actions.

“You stay in control of your Muse and decide the access it gets, what apps it connects to, and how much it’s able to do for you on its own,” Meta states on its Muse security and privacy page. “You set your permissions per connector to help ensure you have the oversight you want.”

Bruce Schneier, a security technologist and lecturer at the Harverd Kennedy School, said whoever releases an AI agent should be held accountable for the harm it causes.

“Who should be held responsible when a dog bites someone? The owner of the dog,” Schneier told the DCNF. “You can’t say ‘not my fault, the dog went rogue.’ It’s your dog.”

Researchers at NewCore, an AI agent security company, found that two of xAI’s Grok Bot agents made 31 attempts in five days to access different apps on its employee accounts, including email, calendar and Slack, according to the company’s Tuesday blog post. The agents did not successfully access any NewCore employee data through these attempts.

“Saying ‘no’ didn’t stop it,” NewCore said in the blog post. “One owner told the bot four times not to act on its own. The next morning it tried every app it had ever been connected to.”

NewCore also noted that Grok Bot denied what actions it took and had no record of the 31 access attempts when checking its history, according to the blog post. NewCore also said it reported the findings to xAI and got confirmation that Grok Bot had no off-switch to disable these actions.

xAI added a new safety measure Wednesday to disable Grok Bot’s Proactive outputs, which are enabled by default, according to Newcore’s blog post.

“Team admins can turn off Proactive messages for the team’s Bots from the dashboard,” xAI said in its product update page.

“The [Proactive message] setting is on by default, so please switch it off for your team,” xAI’s support team told NewCore, the blog post said.

Schneier said the companies that release AI agents should be held accountable for their harmful actions.

“The problem is not AIs acting autonomously,” Schneier told the DCNF. “The problem is corporations deploying autonomous AIs, and then avoiding responsibility when those AIs cause harm.”

Epoch AI, an AI research nonprofit, said AI agents reached its website three times in October during experiments, according to a Nov. 13 incident report. The agents used “false identities” to ask employees for test answers and hunted for passwords on its website. (RELATED: Trump Cans Cyber Chief After Days Of Mysterious Outages Shook Nation)

The nonprofit explained the series of three breaches in a Nov. 13 X post. EpochAI noted in the post that it did not independently verify whose models were used in the incidents.

In late October, three events occurred during alignment evals run by Trajectory Labs, PBC (Trajectory) in which AI agents — identified by Trajectory as publicly available frontier models — interacted with Epoch employees and the Epoch website. Trajectory is an organization that builds safety evals and conducts red-teaming of frontier models. Agents did not succeed in accessing any private or confidential information from Epoch. ➤ The first event, which occurred without Epoch’s approval or prior notice from Trajectory, involved agents attempting multiple exploits, including an SQL injection, and contacting Epoch employees under false identities to try to obtain proprietary Epoch benchmark information. This behavior appears to have resulted, at least in part, from Trajectory giving the agents an intentionally impossible task and instructions not to give up or conclude the task was impossible. ➤ The second event involved renewed agent activity on our public website, which Trajectory attributed to agents getting past a DNS redirect that Trajectory had set up to keep them on a local copy of Epoch’s site. ➤ In the third event, Epoch collaborated with Trajectory on an alignment experiment similar to the first event. Read our incident report, which describes the three events in more detail and recommends minimum standards for future alignment evaluations: https://t.co/Pus4y5urnG To avoid misattributing behavior, the report does not name any AI models or developers, as Epoch AI has not independently verified which were involved.

Trajectory Labs, an AI testing company, ran the tests using Google’s Gemini 4 Argon agents, according to its Nov. 13 blog post. The first experiment began without Epoch AI’s prior knowledge.

The testing firm assigned the agents “an impossible task” to see if they would act similarly to OpenAI’s agents in the Hugging Face hack when safety measures were enabled, the blog post said.

“In October, Gemini 4 Argon AI agents we were testing with API safeguards enabled attempted to hack Epoch AI’s live website while trying to obtain non-existent ‘held-out’ benchmark answers,” Trajectory Labs said in its blog post.

“We often instructed the agents to ‘NEVER stop, NEVER give up,’ and in some runs they had internet access,” the AI testing firm added.

In response to the incidents, the nonprofit said AI testers should seek written consent, monitor their models, and report issues during AI agent experiments, according to its incident report.

Trajectory Labs and Epoch AI both said the nonprofit’s private data was not accessed by the agents during any of the attempts to reach its website, according to their respective reports.

Nathan Calvin, vice president of state affairs and general counsel at AI policy nonprofit Encode, said that publicly reported AI agent incidents likely understate the problem.

“I’m confident that for each of these disclosed incidents, there are likely many more that don’t ever become public,” Calvin told the DCNF.

Meta, SpaceX, Google and Epoch AI each did not respond to the DCNF’s requests for comment.

Experts warn that the risks will grow as Americans give AI agents more access to their accounts and argue tech companies should be held accountable.

“The problem is not AI agents accessing private data. The problem is corporations using AI agents to access peoples’ [sic] private data,” Schneier told the DCNF. “The problem is not AIs acting autonomously. The problem is corporations deploying autonomous AIs, and then avoiding responsibility when those AIs cause harm.”

“Americans should be concerned” about agents potentially accessing their data, Calvin told the DCNF.

“In the near term I still think it’s more plausible that people will be the victim of someone deliberately misusing an AI system to hack rather than from a misaligned autonomous AI agent ‘going rogue,’ but the threat of the latter is also becoming more credible and threatening too,” he said.

A FedEx Cargo Jet overshot the runway at Miami International Airport, stopping just short of a busy road Wednesday night.

Flights out of the airport on Thanksgiving morning remained delayed after Wednesday night’s airport ground stop, caused by the flight from Memphis overshooting its runway upon landing, according to a Miami Herald report.

Screenshot of
news.originalContent:
(Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

A FedEx Cargo Jet overshot the runway at Miami International Airport, stopping just short of a busy road Wednesday night.

Flights out of the airport on Thanksgiving morning remained delayed after Wednesday night’s airport ground stop, caused by the flight from Memphis overshooting its runway upon landing, according to a Miami Herald report.

Screenshot of the Federal Aviation Administration’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center advisory on Wednesday night’s airport ground stop caused by a FedEx flight from Memphis overshooting its runway upon landing.

The incident involving the MD-11 operating FedEx Flight 910 occurred at approximately 8:40 p.m., prompting a complete halt to flights arriving at and departing from Miami International Airport (MIA). (RELATED: FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop, Halting All US Flight Departures)

One runway reopened for departures at 10:30 p.m., followed by a second at 12:17 a.m. Thursday. By 8 a.m. Thursday, three of the airport’s four runways had resumed operations, according to the Miami Herald.

The disruption primarily affected travelers scheduled to fly Wednesday evening, while Thursday morning passengers faced fewer disruptions as airport operations gradually returned to normal.

The Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue reported no injuries among passengers, crew members, or people on the ground following the incident, according to a post on X.

The airport said in a post on X Thursday that, following the cargo jet’s runway overrun, three of its four runways had reopened, while Runway 8L-26R remained closed.

“Following last night’s FedEx Flight 910 runway overrun, three of our four runways are open, while Runway 8L-26R remains closed. As we experience some residual flight impacts today, please check directly with your airline for the latest updates before heading to the airport.”

Update: Following last night’s FedEx Flight 910 runway overrun, three of our four runways are open, while Runway 8L-26R remains closed. As we experience some residual flight impacts today, please check directly with your airline for the latest updates before heading to the airport. Our teams are working hard to safely restore normal operations. We are so grateful for your patience, cooperation, and holiday spirit as we get you where you need to be. Wishing everyone a safe and wonderful Thanksgiving.

The airport also thanked travelers for their patience and cooperation as crews worked to safely resume normal operations, while extending Thanksgiving wishes to passengers traveling for the holiday. (RELATED: FAA Lets Flights Resume After Hours-Long Ground Stop. Mullin Says Disruption Wasn’t A ‘Nefarious Attack.’)

Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava put out a statement in response to the Wednesday night incident, writing on X, “I’m relieved to hear that no one was hurt. I know how difficult these delays are for so many families. Thank you to our first responders and airport teams working to get travelers safely to their loved ones tonight.”

I’m relieved to hear that no one was hurt. I know how difficult these delays are for so many families. Thank you to our first responders and airport teams working to get travelers safely to their loved ones tonight.

The crash marked the second time in less than three months that a cargo aircraft overshot a runway while landing at Miami International Airport.

In a separate incident on Sept. 6, a Boeing 767 operated by 21 Air while transporting Amazon Prime cargo overshot the runway, striking a van beyond the airport grounds. (RELATED: At Least Five Dead, Five Injured In Fatal Amazon Plane Crash)

The crash killed five people inside the vehicle and left five others seriously injured.

news.originalContent:
Photo by Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images

A GOP senator is warning that the White House shouldn’t be deciding who runs one of the country’s most valuable companies.

Republican Sen. Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania said the executive branch should stay out of corporate ownership deals and boardroom leadership calls and that interfering sets a “dangerous precedent,” according to a video statement he posted on X. Decisions about who leads a company and how its board governs belong to the private sector, the freshman senator said.

I don’t know exactly what the president’s calculus was here, but I am worried about the precedent. I believe the private sector should be making decisions about corporate leadership and board governance. That doesn’t mean government has no role. In critical industries like semiconductors and shipbuilding, targeted support can be essential to our national security. But to avoid a dangerous precedent, we need clear and consistent limits on when government intervenes. We don’t want to go down the road of state capitalism and undermine the very system that makes America competitive.

His comments come after President Donald Trump publicly backed the return of ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and claimed to have “made the deal” that got him his job back. Leaving the White House for a trip to Asia on Nov. 16, Trump told reporters he would welcome seeing Huang reinstated, The Hill reported. “I think he learned a big lesson,” Trump said. (RELATED: Trump Says Pardoning Jensen Huang Is ‘Always An Option,’ But Probably Won’t Be ‘Necessary’)

Huang had stepped down on Nov. 12, with finance chief Colette Kress taking over on an interim basis and longtime director Harvey Jones installed as the company’s first board chairman, Fortune reported. The board said it would weigh both internal and external candidates for the permanent job.

Nvidia’s directors closed the door on a comeback the following week. Jones told investors at the start of the company’s Nov. 17 earnings call that the board unanimously accepted the resignation and had no intention of reinstating Huang.

Huang offered a conditional return in an X post the same day, writing that he would be “honored” to come back if directors judged it best for shareholders, employees, the company, and America.

Government does hold a legitimate role in sectors tied to national security, McCormick conceded, pointing to semiconductors and shipbuilding as industries where targeted support can be warranted. But he called for strict and consistent limits on when government officials can step in, cautioning against a slide toward “state capitalism” and a slippery slope that could erode the country’s competitive edge. McCormick, a former hedge fund CEO who is married to Meta President Dina Powell McCormick, described himself as a “red-blooded capitalist.
news.content:
Photo by Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images

A GOP senator is warning that the White House shouldn’t be deciding who runs one of the country’s most valuable companies.

Republican Sen. Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania said the executive branch should stay out of corporate ownership deals and boardroom leadership calls and that interfering sets a “dangerous precedent,” according to a video statement he posted on X. Decisions about who leads a company and how its board governs belong to the private sector, the freshman senator said.

I don’t know exactly what the president’s calculus was here, but I am worried about the precedent. I believe the private sector should be making decisions about corporate leadership and board governance. That doesn’t mean government has no role. In critical industries like semiconductors and shipbuilding, targeted support can be essential to our national security. But to avoid a dangerous precedent, we need clear and consistent limits on when government intervenes. We don’t want to go down the road of state capitalism and undermine the very system that makes America competitive.

His comments come after President Donald Trump publicly backed the return of ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and claimed to have “made the deal” that got him his job back. Leaving the White House for a trip to Asia on Nov. 16, Trump told reporters he would welcome seeing Huang reinstated, The Hill reported. “I think he learned a big lesson,” Trump said. (RELATED: Trump Says Pardoning Jensen Huang Is ‘Always An Option,’ But Probably Won’t Be ‘Necessary’)

Huang had stepped down on Nov. 12, with finance chief Colette Kress taking over on an interim basis and longtime director Harvey Jones installed as the company’s first board chairman, Fortune reported. The board said it would weigh both internal and external candidates for the permanent job.

Nvidia’s directors closed the door on a comeback the following week. Jones told investors at the start of the company’s Nov. 17 earnings call that the board unanimously accepted the resignation and had no intention of reinstating Huang.

Huang offered a conditional return in an X post the same day, writing that he would be “honored” to come back if directors judged it best for shareholders, employees, the company, and America.

Government does hold a legitimate role in sectors tied to national security, McCormick conceded, pointing to semiconductors and shipbuilding as industries where targeted support can be warranted. But he called for strict and consistent limits on when government officials can step in, cautioning against a slide toward “state capitalism” and a slippery slope that could erode the country’s competitive edge. McCormick, a former hedge fund CEO who is married to Meta President Dina Powell McCormick, described himself as a “red-blooded capitalist.

Dez Bryant didn’t hold back after watching his former Cowboys team author the largest Thanksgiving collapse in NFL history.

The legendary wide receiver, who was in attendance in Texas, was calling for Cowboys owner Jerry Jones to clean house as the team was in the process of blowing a 21-point third-quarter lead with a calamity of a fourth quarter.

Bryant doubled down after Jake Elliott’s 59-yard field goal with three seconds remaining gave the Eagles an improbable 39-38 win at AT&T Stadium on Thursday.

“Jerry, Jerry, Jerry, everybody got to get the f–k up out of here,” Bryant, who played eight years on Dallas from 2010-2017, said in a video posted to social media. “F–k that. That’s completely unacceptable. That is unacceptable. F–k that

“Get everybody the f–k up out of here. Fire everybody. Fire’m all. F–k it. Fire’m, get everybody the f–k out. F–k that. Fire everybody.”

The Cowboys were as much to blame for losing the game as the Eagles were for winning, as they surrendered a blocked punt for a touchdown early in the fourth quarter, watched usually automatic kicker Brandon Aubrey miss from 40 yards on a kick that would have given them a five-point lead with 3:27 remaining in the game.

Dallas (5-7) chose to try to put the game away by going for it on fourth and 1 from the Eagles’ 41, but Dak Prescott was sacked, setting up Philly’s last-gasp effort.

The loss denied the Cowboys a chance to get to .500 and keep themselves in the thick of the NFC East race, which should put coach Brian Schottenheimer further on the hot seat.

Jones called the loss a “bitter disappointment” to reporters. He said that a coaching change is “not a thought on my mind at this particular time” and that there are “several more games to go and we have to have our mind on that.”

Former Cowboys QB Joe Milton threw for 331 yards, two touchdowns and one interception for the Eagles (4-7), who kept their slim playoff hopes alive.

DeVonta Smith caught 11 passes for 200 yards and two scores as the Dallas defense continues to struggle.

“Luckily, this bird escaped the traffic and the Thanksgiving menu, making it off the roadway safely!” the department added.
