پس از انتشار ویدئو و در خردادماه گذشته، دادگاه کیفری استان قم با استناد به موادی از قانون مجازات اسلامی از جمله ماده ۶۳۸ این قانون و ماده ۷۴۳ قانون جرایم رایانه‌ای، برای خانم احمدی و دست‌اندرکاران این «کنسرت مجازی» پرونده قضایی تشکیل و شعبه ۱۲۲ دادگاه کیفری دو قم آنان را به اتهام «جریحه‌دار کردن عفت عمومی از طریق تولید و انتشار محتوای مبتذل و خلاف اخلاق در فضای مجازی» به هر یک ۷۴ ضربه شلاق تعزیری، دو سال محرومیت از فعالیت‌های هنری و موسیقایی و دو سال ممنوعیت خروج از کشور محکوم کرد.

اتهام مطرح‌شده علیه آنان «جریحه‌دار کردن عفت عمومی از طریق تولید و انتشار محتوای مبتذل و خلاف اخلاق در بستر فضای مجازی» عنوان شد.

به گفته آقای نیلی شعبه ۱۶ دادگاه تجدیدنظر استان قم این حکم را تایید کرده و پرونده برای اجرا به اجرای احکام فرستاده شده که «امروز حکم شلاق پنج نفر از محکومان اجرا شده است.»

در سوم مهر امسال عباس قرآباغی، رئیس شعبه ۱۶ دادگاه تجدیدنظر قم، در حکم صادره، مدارک و استدلال‌های ارائه شده از سوی وکلای پرونده را کافی ندانسته است و رای دادگاه بدوی را تایید کرده بود.

امیرعلی پیرنیا؛ علیرضا بچاری، مجید محسنی، سهیل فقیه نصیری، محمد امین طاهری، محسن لشکری و تهمینه منزوی سایر اعضای گروهی هستند که کنسرت مجازی کاروان را سال ۱۴۰۳ تولید و منتشر کردند.

احسان بیرق‌دار، یکی دیگر از همکاران این کنسرت تقاضای تجدید نظر نکرده بود.

دادگاه تجدیدنظر استان قم، در حکم خود نظر دادگاه بدوی را «کافی و متقن» خوانده بود.

«کنسرت کاروانسرا» تنها در فاصله چند ساعت پس از انتشار در یوتیوب بیش از ۱۰۰ هزار بازدید داشت و بخش‌هایی از آن به‌طور گسترده در شبکه‌های اجتماعی بازنشر شد.

ویدئوی اصلی این اجرا میلیون‌ها بار بازدید داشت و کلیپ‌های جداشده از آن نیز به‌طور گسترده در فضای مجازی دست‌به‌دست شده‌اند.

پرستو احمدی پیش‌تر درباره این کنسرت در کانال یوتیوب خود نوشته بود: «من، پرستو؛ دختری که می‌خواهم برای مردمی که دوستشان دارم بخوانم. این حقی است که نمی‌توانستم از آن چشم بپوشم.»

برگزاری این کنسرت هم‌زمان با برخوردهای قضایی و امنیتی با زنان مخالف حجاب اجباری در ایران انجام شده بود.

news.originalContent:

Monday’s arrest of a heavily-armed man planning a violent revolution against the government to oppose Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is yet another achievement for federal prosecutor Bill Essayli and the FBI.

But the arrest is also a giant warning flag about the policies of outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom, incoming Rep. Scott Wiener, and other Democrats.

Just last week, a federal judge struck down two anti-ICE laws that Wiener proposed and that Newsom signed into law.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

The laws would have required ICE agents to wear identifying badges, and would have barred them from wearing masks to hide their identities.

It should have been obvious to anyone that forcing ICE agents to reveal who they are would have exposed them to grave danger.

The anti-ICE activists are fanatical, well-organized, and prone to violence — as we saw in last year’s riots.

Earlier this year, two anti-ICE influencers stalked an ICE agent, and livestreamed their hunt as they followed him to his home. They were tried and convicted, but there are others who would try to do the same.

Monday’s arrest is a case in point.

The would-be revolutionary tried to look up three ICE agents, and researched a leaked federal database.

If the FBI had not caught him in time, he might have carried out terrible acts of cruelty and destruction.

Newsom and Wiener would have made such attacks far easier to carry out.

They had to know the risk they were taking with the lives of federal law enforcement officers.

They did not care — nor did they care about whether what they were doing was constitutional.

They simply wanted to appease anti-ICE sentiments within the Democratic electorate. Wiener was facing off against left-wing opponents in the race for Nancy Pelosi’s seat, and Newsom is preparing a likely campaign for president.

But neither Wiener nor Newsom should be able to live down what they tried to do.

You can oppose the Trump administration’s immigration policies without putting a target on the backs of the men and women who protect this country.

Every country has borders. Those borders need to be enforced. And that enforcement extends into the interior.

That’s because some people aren’t caught at the border, and because some people arrive legally but stay illegally.

That’s the reported reason behind the recent ICE arrests of two Mexican nationals at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. The disturbing video of the arrest in front of fellow airline passengers made its way around social media.

ICE alleges that one of the detainees assaulted officers by throwing hot coffee at them.

Again, you can disagree with ICE’s tactics. But violence is never the answer.

Essayli sent a message. Let’s hope Newsom and Wiener received it.

The Cincinnati Zoo has made drastic safety changes to its “Hippo Cove” following the tragic death of Fiona the hippo last week.

The zoo’s hippo habitat reopened Monday after being closed since Fiona, the 9-year-old adorable hippo, died Thursday from accidentally swallowing a knitted cap that was tossed into her enclosure, according to the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden.

Following the social media star’s sudden death, the Cincinnati Zoo plans to install new safeguards to  prevent objects from entering the enclosure in hopes of stopping such a “freak event” from ever happening again, zoo officials said.

“Even though the habitat already met strict standards set by the AZA [Association of Zoos and Aquariums], we made some modifications to guard against something like this ever happening again,” Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a statement.

“We added a layer of netting above the viewing windows and, out of an abundance of caution, removed all ceiling fans in the area.”

Association President Dan Ashe added that nothing could have foreseen that a visitor at the zoo would toss the hat in the air — causing a ceiling fan to catch it and fling it through a small opening above the windows of Fiona’s enclosure on Nov. 8.

The hat became lodged in Fiona’s small intestine, making it impossible to remove, her necropsy determined.

“The Cincinnati Zoo has been accredited since 1978 and was last accredited in 2025 after an exhaustive inspection, a standard practice for Zoos seeking or renewing accreditation,” Ashe said.

“Nothing was of concern for the hippo habitat in the inspection report. It seems like it was a freak event that couldn’t have been foreseen. Our hearts go out to all the professionals at the Cincinnati Zoo. I know they are devastated by this.”

Other hippos in the enclosure, including Fiona’s mom, 27-year-old Bibi, and Fiona’s 4-year-old brother, Fritz, have been getting extra care and pumpkin treats in Hippo Cove, and are behaving normally, according to the zoo’s director of animal care.

The zoo still urged visitors to secure their belongings, take extra care while near animal habitats, and alert staff immediately if they see something unusual.

Fiona, who was born prematurely in 2017, captured the hearts of animal lovers who followed her viral progress after being born drastically underweight and too small to stand and nurse from her mom.

“Fiona’s story of survival captured the hearts of millions of people all over the world,” Ashe said.

“Her death has the potential to do the same thing. It’s an opportunity for all us to think about our impacts on the natural world and the animals that occupy it.”

WASHINGTON — Melania Trump kicked off the holiday season with the delivery of the White House Christmas Tree, an event thanking the military, and a call for peace.

“America’s children must inherit peace,” she said at a Red Cross event to assemble care packages for the military.

Wearing a festive red-and-white plaid Gabriela Hearst coat, the first lady joined military spouses to assemble boxes of treats. Second lady Usha Vance; Katie Miller, wife of chief of staff Stephen Miller; and Jennifer Hegseth, wife of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, also lent a helping hand.

Trump and Vance walked around the hangar at Joint Base Andrews where the event was taking place, chatting with volunteers and pausing at different stations to help with assembly.

At one point they almost ran into each other, laughing as they moved around each other to continue mingling with the volunteers.

The packages consisted of treats — pretzels, rice crispy treats, and candy.  Each box requires 34 stamps for delivery.

The two ladies capped the event by signing holiday cards for the troops.

“Thank you for your service. Be safe. Happy Thanksgiving,” the first lady wrote in her cards.

“Thank you so much for taking care of all of us! We are so grateful,” was the message from Usha Vance.

The holiday season has officially begun at the White House. Christmas wreaths filled the windows of the executive mansion. Staff hung lights and garland in their offices.

Trump selected the theme “American Bloom” for the holiday decor at the White House. It will be unveiled after Thanksgiving.

The first lady on Monday also received an 18-foot concolor fir from Silent Night Evergreens in Endeavor, Wisconsin, which will have the honor of being the official White House Christmas Tree.

A horse-drawn carriage brought the tree up the driveway. The first lady walked around to inspect it before thanking the Chapman family, whose farm provided the tree. She also thanked Chuck Jensen, a 10-year U.S. Army veteran and FedEx Freight driver, who transported the tree to Washington, D.C.

One of Taylor Swift’s former classmates called her out for being a bully — completely refuting the singer’s narrative that she was an outcast during her school years.

In a savage takedown piece published by Vanity Fair Monday, the outlet contrasts what the pop star has said about her own upbringing with what people (who allegedly knew her in real life) claim is the more accurate picture of her character.

While Swift has claimed in past interviews that she had no friends when she was younger and was left out of social gatherings, Chanice Skinner — a classmate who sat by her in music class at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High in Pennsylvania — alleged the singer was “always part of the popular crowd.”

“If you weren’t part of her friend group, you didn’t exist to her,” Skinner claimed to Vanity Fair.

Skinner then recalled her reaction to Swift’s 2010 Target commercial, in which she talks about being bullied.

“I was like, ‘You were part of that. What are you talking about? If anything, you were one of the bullies,'” Skinner said of Swift.

Start your day with Page Six Daily.

Additionally, Sharon Luyben, who was the teacher of the music class, also refuted Swift’s 2009 interview with Katie Couric, in which the Grammy winner recalled a brutal story of her friends no longer wanting to associate with her when she was around 12 years old.

In the interview, Swift claimed that when she would sit by her friends at lunch, they would pick up their food and move to another table.

Luyben bluntly alleged to Vanity Fair, “That wasn’t true. We had assigned seating in junior high.”

The bullying tactics remained even after Swift got famous, according to a music industry executive, dubbed “The Exec” in the piece.

“It’s truly Regina George,” they claimed, referencing the calculating “Mean Girls” character played by Rachel McAdams in the 2004 film.

Referencing Swift’s reported feud with Charli XCX — who the author refers to as “The Brat” in the piece — The Exec says Swift has “done this performance that she’s supportive of her…but she’s not.”

The piece accuses her of pulling similar tactics with Olivia Rodrigo — dubbed “The Protégé” — and Katy Perry, who is referred to as “The California Girl.”

The Exec also claims that Swift’s friends are not allowed to collaborate with her rivals, and that her rivals are also not allowed to interact with her social world.

Some of the allegations and opinions made against Swift in the piece were from unnamed sources who spoke to Vanity Fair. Swift’s rep did not immediately respond to Page Six’s request for comment.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Are you ready to uncover the truth about the culprit at the end of Dig Season 1? See what we did there?

**Spoiler alert: This article contains details about Dig Season 1, now streaming on Peacock**

If you tuned into the first season of Amy Poehler and Mike Schur‘s new team-up, their follow-up to Parks and Recreation, you might have been surprised by the mystery element that is introduced early on in the series. Episode 4 of the comedy ends with the revelation that the statue Elise (Poehler) and her gang of ragtag gals had discovered — a monument depicting Hera, which they aptly nicknamed “Pretty Woman” to speak in code around the camp — had been stolen from their pit. In a way, the series becomes more like another one of Schur’s more recent shows, i.e., A Man on the Inside or The Good Place, which cracks jokes at a mile-a-minute pace while also leaving the audience guessing about how the characters and storylines have ended up where they do.

Luckily, just like with Schur’s Netflix comedy mystery starring Ted Danson, the Season 1 finale of Dig provides the answers the audience so desperately needs about the big questions of the season, including why someone would take a precious and world-changing artifact from a dig site and how they did it.

Thankfully, even if you didn’t make it to the end, we’ve got you covered with all the answers. Keep reading for a full breakdown of the Season 1 ending of Dig, including who stole Pretty Woman, where they hid the statue, and why they did it…

In the end, it was none other than the dig site overseer, Neville Wycombe (Hugh Laurie), who was behind the theft of the ancient artifact, as he had planned to move Pretty Woman through back channels and sell the statue to keep the dig site alive. According to Neville, enthusiasm for such expeditions had dried up over the years, and selling smaller pieces and discoveries on the black market over the years had allowed him to fund their operations without ever alerting anyone to any suspicious activity. As for how he stole the statue, it turns out that deception is Neville’s weapon of choice, rather than strength.

While the entire season had seen Elise, Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), Patty (Fina Strazza), and Clare (Antonia Thomas) questioning how anyone would be able to move a massive and heavy monument out of the ground without catching the attention of the camper at the dig site, it turns out that Pretty Woman never even left the pit in the first place.

It’s only after Patty goes out to the pit to have her first official kiss that she notices someone filled the hole in by a few inches, which causes Elise to realize that Pretty Woman had not been stolen, just covered with a thin layer of dirt and sand to make it look like she had been removed. In reality, Neville’s plan was to wait until all of the campers had left for the summer and then take the priceless relic out of the pit without raising any suspicion.

Unfortunately for Elise and the gang, before they are able to alert the authorities to Neville’s master plan, he discovers them in the trench and puts the kabosh on their plan, only for the camp administrator, Dorothy (Bonita Friedricy), to storm the site with a loaded pistol in hand. After using Dorothy as a fall guy in the theft and promising to buy her a plot of land in the Cotswolds, Dorothy learns that Neville had never actually planned to help her make her dreams of a dog sanctuary come true, which results in her showing up to threaten him at gunpoint.

Before Dorothy is able to shoot Neville, however, the excitement of the discovery mixed with the pressure of being held with a gun pointed at him causes him to have a second, larger heart attack following the smaller one at the beginning of the season, leading him to fall backwards into the trench, nearly dead. Shocked at Neville’s sudden collapse (and not knowing how to use a gun), Dorothy accidentally shoots Neville’s lifeless body twice as the rest of the group scrambles to figure out what to do with the sticky situation.

That ultimately leads us to the scene that kicks off the series, which includes Clare biting Elise in the arm, Elise punching Dylan, and Patty shooting herself in the leg. Why, you might ask? To cover their tracks, of course! The group realizes that the only way to save themselves from all going to prison is to make it look like they fought off looters at the site and report the discovery of Pretty Woman while also calling in the police to come and retrieve Neville’s body.

One last thing: Neville isn’t dead! While being questioned by the police, Elise learns that Neville somehow survived the heart attack (and the gunshot wounds), which is when she visits him in the hospital and tells him that the jig is up. In exchange for not turning him in to the authorities, Elise tells Neville that he must retire and never try to sell another piece again, which he begrudgingly agrees to. The season ends with Elise, Dylan, Clare, and Patty going their separate ways but leaving the door open on further adventures (or should we say, misadventures), in a potential Season 2?

Dig Season 1 is now streaming on Peacock.

Peacock currently offers two subscription types: Premium with ads and Premium Plus ad-free. Peacock Premium costs $12.99/month, while Premium Plus costs $19.99/month.

You can save a bit by subscribing to one of Peacock’s annual plans, which give you 12 months for the price of 10. These cost either $129.99 with ads or $199.99 without ads.

Peacock Premium Plus is also available to subscribe to via Prime Video with a seven-day free trial that you can’t get by subscribing directly on Peacock.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A new New York City K-through-12 school boasts six dance studios, a rooftop field, middle schoolers working on logic problems taken from the LSAT and high schoolers taking five AP classes and eyeing Ivy League schools.

It’s not a fancy private school on the Upper East Side but rather the first standalone campus for a Success Academy. Launched in 2006, the network of charter schools has always used existing buildings and shared campuses with traditional public schools.

The new Bronx campus, which opened this past August and serves 2,400 children admitted through a random lottery rather than an entrance exam, is its first real outpost built from the ground up. Success Academy founder and CEO Eva Moskowitz decided to build the new school in the poorest congressional district in the nation to prove a point.

“There’s nothing wrong with the children,” Moskowitz told me during a visit to the campus earlier this month. “There’s something wrong with the system that fails to deliver for kids and families now going on a half-century.”

The school is housed within a stunningly beautiful, six-story, 300,000-square-foot structure that contains a 300-seat auditorium, two-story gymnasium, ceramics studios and outdoor rooftop terraces.

“Children deserve a building like this,” Moskowitz said.

It cost a reported $245 million to build. Moskowitz said it could have cost more than twice as much to build with the School Construction Authority, the public agency responsible for Dept. of Education construction. Since Success Academy isn’t subject to the same regulations as union schools, it can be nimbler with building.

For Audrey, a high school junior whose favorite subject is AP physics and who has been a Success student since third grade, the new campus is her favorite part of coming to school.

“It’s the first time we’re having a whole school to ourselves … every day you see something new around this beautiful campus,” she enthused.

Success isn’t just showing how schools can be built better and for less money, it is also upending the traditional criticisms of charter schools — that they handpick the best students or rely on small classroom sizes to achieve impressive results.

“Ninety-four percent of our kids are kids of color, and our schools are located in the most economically disadvantaged areas of the city,” Moskowitz says. Teachers have 40 kids in their classrooms on average, and those children are selected randomly.

Success Academy cultivates what it calls “a culture of excellence” with strict rules and high expectations.

School typically starts at 7:30 a.m. and runs until 4:30 p.m. —  a long day compared to typical public schools, which run from 8:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. The extra hours aren’t just about fitting in more academics; they also make room for chess, dance, theater, sports and art throughout the day. The school calls them co-curriculars rather than extracurriculars because they’re treated as equal in importance to academics — the kinds of opportunities that only affluent children typically have access to.

Excessive absences and tardies are not tolerated and can lead to a student being forced to repeat a grade.

“We’re old-fashioned … you used to have to get to school on time,” Moskowitz said. And students internalize that expectation. “If you’re in Harlem at 7:30 a.m., you will see a little kid drag their parent running down the block because they want to get to school on time.”

Shannon Beatty, who is the principal at the new location, said by the time she arrives at 6:30 a.m. each morning, kids are already lined up. Teachers will also call parents starting at 6:45 a.m. if they feel that a family needs a nudge.

“It’s possible to not only have high standards, but also to insist that kids can meet those standards,” Beatty said. “Right now, that [belief] is what’s lacking in other schools.”

Gentility — or what Moskowitz calls “habits of the mind” — is also a point of focus. Elementary students move between rooms quietly and without running. In lieu of a bell that indicates changing classes, Success plays various selections of classical music.

Students learn to say “please” and “thank you,” to write neatly and to craft professional emails.

The academic expectations start early: students study logic in second grade, and Moskowitz said many middle-school logic problems come from the LSAT. All students are required to take AP classes, starting in the eighth grade. Many tackle a heavy load — Audrey took five AP exams as a freshman.

“Kids don’t come out of the womb caring about their musical success, their athletic success, their academic success,” Moskowitz explained. “You have to build a culture where winning and achieving is something that’s pleasurable for kids.”

Moskowitz, a former city councilwoman, opened the first Success Academy in Harlem 20 years ago with 165 kindergartners and first graders, and served as its principal.

“I wasn’t building schools for black kids or Latin kids. I was trying to build world-class schools that any parent would want to send their kid to,” said Moskowitz, who did in fact send her own children to Success Academy.

She also believes in ignoring trends and sticking with what works.

Moskowitz said teachers unions — “and the elected officials who do their bidding” — have been one of their greatest impediments. The United Federation of Teachers and its state affiliates have sued repeatedly over everything from their use of DOE buildings to the creation of new charters.

“It has been a battle royale,” Moskowitz said. “They see us as competition to a monopolistic system.”

When she was on City Council, Moskowitz held hearings on teachers’, principals’ and custodians’ union contracts while chairing the education committee. She believes that scrutiny — and her politics — helped make her a target.

Moskowitz says Success received 58,000 applications in a recent hiring cycle to hire fewer than 1,000 teachers. Yet some applicants struggled with the very material they would be expected to teach — teachers struggling to do the fifth-grade math they need to have mastered.

Success has announced plans to build a graduate school of education to better school teachers.

It’s also expanding its presence beyond New York City for the first time — spreading to Florida where five new elementary schools are slated to open in fall 2027.

“We’re a can-do country, and yet we’ve almost given up on our children. Why would we do that?” Moskowitz said. “We don’t have to accept educational dysfunction. We really don’t. And morally we can’t afford to.”

A new New York City K-through-12 school boasts six dance studios, a rooftop field, middle schoolers working on logic problems taken from the LSAT and high schoolers taking five AP classes and eyeing Ivy League schools.

It’s not a fancy private school on the Upper East Side but rather the first standalone campus for a Success Academy. Launched in 2006, the network of charter schools has always used existing buildings and shared campuses with traditional public schools.

The school is housed within a stunningly beautiful, six-story, 300,000-square-foot structure that contains a 300-seat auditorium, two-story gymnasium, ceramics studios and outdoor rooftop terraces.

“Children deserve a building like this,” Moskowitz said.

news.originalContent:
US Treasury sanctions more than two dozen Iranian entities, citing efforts to disrupt Tehran’s global financial activities, amid ongoing diplomatic effort to end the US-Israel war on Iran.

The United States has launched another wave of sanctions against Iran under its Operation Economic Outcast, a move that comes shortly after US President Donald Trump threatened renewed military action next year.

The Department of the Treasury announced on Monday that it had targeted more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel with sanctions “in a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran’s global shadow banking networks”.

“Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime,” said US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent.

The US Treasury claimed these entities help Iran “move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions”.

Bessent also vowed the “Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake.”

The Central Bank of Iran oversees the designated entities, according to the statement.

The designated entities include an Iran-based company named “Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company (Nesim Baharan)”, which the Treasury claims worked closely with Iranian exchange houses and their front companies to facilitate transactions on behalf of Sarmayeh Bank’s Iranian clients, which include major Iranian petrochemical companies.

In addition, “Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company (Fashki Exchange) and Mellat Exchange Company” and a number of their owners and employees were designated.

The US claimed earlier this month that its sanctions campaign had pushed Iran’s rial to new lows and driven inflation to about 90 percent.

AP reported that Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran still hoped diplomacy could end its nine-month war with the US, while President Trump said Iran wanted a deal, but one that was not acceptable to him.

Fox News said Trump told its chief foreign correspondent that he was “inclined to order military strikes against Iran after the new year if the two countries fail to reach an agreement”.

The remarks came as diplomatic efforts continued to end a conflict that has destabilised the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up global energy prices, and drawn in countries across the region.

news.originalContent:
Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday, accusing the company of promoting Grok’s ‘spicy mode’.

The US states of Virginia and Oregon have sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX, saying the business harmed consumers by avoiding safeguards when it designed and launched an artificial intelligence chatbot capable of creating sexualised images.

The attorneys general of both states filed complaints in separate lawsuits on Monday.

Several states had announced investigations into Grok over similar claims in recent months, but Virginia and Oregon are the first states to sue.

The lawsuits filed in state courts accuse SpaceX of misleading consumers about Grok’s safety and failing to put adequate safeguards in place while promoting its “spicy mode”. The feature allows users to take an existing photograph of a person and generate a sexual or nude image or video, according to the lawsuits.

The company prioritised its business model over the safety of millions of people, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in his state’s lawsuit.

“To push its lagging product, Grok, to tens of millions of new users, it stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a ‘spicy mode’ built to produce nudity,” Jones said in the lawsuit. “For these Defendants, weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature.”

Virginia and Oregon accused SpaceX of violating their respective consumer protection laws. They are seeking damages, penalties and court orders forcing the company to stop violating state law.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Grok is available to users of X, the social media platform that is a subsidiary of SpaceX.

In a statement posted on X on Monday that did not directly address the lawsuits, the platform’s safety team said it had taken action to block prompts that could generate sexualised or nude imagery and worked with law enforcement to pursue people who use the platform to make it.

“The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards,” the company posted.

Virginia’s lawsuit cites data from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate, which estimated that between December 2025 and January 2026, Grok generated and posted millions of sexualised images on X, including more than 20,000 depicting children.

Investigators from the attorney general’s office in Virginia found that Grok’s image moderation was inconsistent, and that the bot would advise users on how to circumvent the moderation measures by avoiding words that triggered it, according to the lawsuit.

Beginning in January, Grok told users that its image generation features were only for paying subscribers, which did not stop the images’ creation but allowed the company to profit from them, the lawsuit said.

SpaceX is facing more than a dozen lawsuits brought by individuals who say nonconsensual sexual images of them as minors or adults were generated by Grok.

news.originalContent:
Despite working and having health insurance, some of the country’s sickest patients have trouble affording the medicines they need.

Sarah Wisniewski and her sister were once contemplating an extraordinary arrangement to manage their shared multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnoses: alternating months taking a life-changing medication.

The drug, which Wisniewski says costs thousands of dollars a month without insurance coverage, was so expensive that the sisters considered rationing their treatment rather than going without it entirely.

“It’s a weird thing to have to think about,” the 45-year-old told Al Jazeera. “You go to college, you get insurance, you get a good job, you pay your bills, you do everything right and, still, you’re having to ration your medication.”

Wisniewski is one of more than four in 10 adults in the United States who did not take medication as prescribed last year because of the cost, estimates KFF, an independent health policy research organisation.

Her experience highlights the growing financial pressures facing some of the nation’s sickest patients, who have trouble affording costly prescription medications, despite having jobs and private health insurance.

Wisniewski was diagnosed with MS in 2017 after experiencing increasingly debilitating symptoms, including difficulties with her vision, mobility and breathing.

She became one of the nearly eight in 10 American adults who are living with at least one chronic condition, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In the summer of 2024, her neurologist prescribed Kesimpta, a medication that, she says, dramatically improved her condition. But her insurance company, Blue Cross Blue Shield, notified her it would not cover the treatment.

Wisniewski appealed three times before requesting a hearing in her state of Maryland. Only weeks before that hearing was due to take place did her insurer agree to cover the medication.

Without that intervention, Wisniewski said, she would have faced a monthly bill of approximately $10,000.

The impact of obtaining treatment has been significant on her life.

“I went from barely being able to walk … Now, I walk my dog every morning, a mile-and-a-half to two miles,” she said.

Wisniewski has also been able to maintain her federal contracting job, which she described as highly technical and demanding.

But the financial burden remains substantial. Even with the help of insurance, Wisniewski estimates she spends between $800 and $900 each month on medication.

“Almost every spare dime I get is going to just keeping me healthy, so I can make it to work the next day,” she said.

Unlike many countries, particularly wealthier ones, the US allows pharmaceutical companies significantly more latitude to set their own prices.

According to the Patients For Affordable Drugs Now patient-advocacy organisation, current laws give manufacturers “unilateral power to set launch prices in the US and the ability to raise prices at will”.

“I believe this is a uniquely American problem, ”Wisniewski said. “Other countries are …  able to provide for their citizens these drugs, if not for free, at an affordable level.”

The monthly cost of her medication in Canada is 2,333 Canadian dollars ($1,623). It’s even lower in Australia at 41 Australian dollars ($27) or 6.60 Australian dollars ($4.37) with a concession card, which allows eligible residents in the country to receive discounts on healthcare and prescription medicines.

The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA), a consortium that represents US drug companies, argues that a complicated network of third-party middlemen, known as pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and insurance companies are to blame for the country’s high drug prices.

“PBMs and insurers control benefits through processes like prior authorisation, embedded step therapy, and formulary controls that may allow PBMs and insurers to deny coverage or push patients to alternative treatments from the initially prescribed medicine,” PhRMA’s website said. The organisation did not reply to a request for comment.

A study by the nonpartisan RAND organisation, released in 2024, found that US prescription drug prices were substantially higher than those in other wealthy countries, particularly for name-brand medications.

Using 2022 data, RAND’s researchers found that US manufacturers’ gross prices across all prescription drugs were 278 percent higher than the average prices in 33 other high-income countries. For brand-name drugs, US prices were more than four times the comparison-country average.

But the consequences of the current US system can extend far beyond the cost of individual prescriptions.

Wisniewski said the money she spends maintaining access to medication is money she cannot put toward local businesses, transportation or investments in her community.

“I really think that a lot of people, at an abstract level, understand that this could happen to anybody at any point in time,” she said. “But I don’t think that it really hits home to folks that you are legitimately one bad phone call away from losing everything.”

After this month’s historic midterm elections in the US, where Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress by wide margins, there will be few areas of agreement with Democrats’ Republican counterparts – and President Donald Trump.

But targeted reforms that address the high cost of prescriptions could be an area where both parties find common ground.

A survey conducted by Fabrizio Ward in March 2025 found more than three in four voters – including 70 percent of Trump supporters – wanted Congress to take action on reducing drug prices.

The issue was the focus of a US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday of last week, when lawmakers and healthcare experts examined how pharmaceutical companies and insurers influence pricing and access to medication.

At that November 17 hearing, witnesses highlighted several factors contributing to high prescription drug costs, including pharmaceutical patent protections and the role of PBMs.

Merith Basey, chief executive officer of Patients For Affordable Drugs Now, argued that pharmaceutical companies exploit the patent system to delay competition from cheaper alternatives.

One of those practices, known as patent thicketing, involves companies securing multiple patents covering different aspects of a medication or its delivery device, potentially making it more difficult for competitors to introduce generic alternatives.

Basey told lawmakers the introduction of generic competition could substantially reduce prices, arguing a single generic competitor can lower a drug’s price by 39 percent, while six or more competitors can reduce prices by as much as 95 percent.

But other witnesses pointed to PBMs, claiming their involvement in distributing drugs can influence pricing.

The Senate panel has advanced a number of proposals to tackle the high cost of prescription drugs in the US. One of those is the bipartisan Eliminating Thickets to Improve Competition (ETHIC) Act, which would limit the practice of patent thickening, making it easier for generic drugs to enter the US market and lower costs.

“Big Pharma knows exactly what it’s doing in monopolising the US patent system: driving up drug costs for Americans while preventing generic-drug manufacturers from getting their foot in the market,” Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, one of the bill’s sponsors, said in a statement.

Wisniewski noted that while the ETHIC Act wouldn’t make her prescription “cheap”, it would be “astronomically better than what we have now”.

Wisniewski is one of more than four in 10 adults in the United States who did not take medication as prescribed last year because of the cost, estimates KFF, an independent health policy research organisation.

Her experience highlights the growing financial pressures facing some of the nation’s sickest patients, who have trouble affording costly prescription medications, despite having jobs and private health insurance.

Wisniewski was diagnosed with MS in 2017 after experiencing increasingly debilitating symptoms, including difficulties with her vision, mobility and breathing.

She became one of the nearly eight in 10 American adults who are living with at least one chronic condition, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In the summer of 2024, her neurologist prescribed Kesimpta, a medication that, she says, dramatically improved her condition. But her insurance company, Blue Cross Blue Shield, notified her it would not cover the treatment.

Wisniewski appealed three times before requesting a hearing in her state of Maryland. Only weeks before that hearing was due to take place did her insurer agree to cover the medication.

Without that intervention, Wisniewski said, she would have faced a monthly bill of approximately $10,000.

The impact of obtaining treatment has been significant on her life.

“I went from barely being able to walk … Now, I walk my dog every morning, a mile-and-a-half to two miles,” she said.

Wisniewski has also been able to maintain her federal contracting job, which she described as highly technical and demanding.

But the financial burden remains substantial. Even with the help of insurance, Wisniewski estimates she spends between $800 and $900 each month on medication.

“Almost every spare dime I get is going to just keeping me healthy, so I can make it to work the next day,” she said.

Unlike many countries, particularly wealthier ones, the US allows pharmaceutical companies significantly more latitude to set their own prices.

According to the Patients For Affordable Drugs Now patient-advocacy organisation, current laws give manufacturers “unilateral power to set launch prices in the US and the ability to raise prices at will”.

“I believe this is a uniquely American problem, ”Wisniewski said. “Other countries are …  able to provide for their citizens these drugs, if not for free, at an affordable level.”

The monthly cost of her medication in Canada is 2,333 Canadian dollars ($1,623). It’s even lower in Australia at 41 Australian dollars ($27) or 6.60 Australian dollars ($4.37) with a concession card, which allows eligible residents in the country to receive discounts on healthcare and prescription medicines.

The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA), a consortium that represents US drug companies, argues that a complicated network of third-party middlemen, known as pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and insurance companies are to blame for the country’s high drug prices.

“PBMs and insurers control benefits through processes like prior authorisation, embedded step therapy, and formulary controls that may allow PBMs and insurers to deny coverage or push patients to alternative treatments from the initially prescribed medicine,” PhRMA’s website said. The organisation did not reply to a request for comment.

A study by the nonpartisan RAND organisation, released in 2024, found that US prescription drug prices were substantially higher than those in other wealthy countries, particularly for name-brand medications.

Using 2022 data, RAND’s researchers found that US manufacturers’ gross prices across all prescription drugs were 278 percent higher than the average prices in 33 other high-income countries. For brand-name drugs, US prices were more than four times the comparison-country average.

But the consequences of the current US system can extend far beyond the cost of individual prescriptions.

Wisniewski said the money she spends maintaining access to medication is money she cannot put toward local businesses, transportation or investments in her community.

“I really think that a lot of people, at an abstract level, understand that this could happen to anybody at any point in time,” she said. “But I don’t think that it really hits home to folks that you are legitimately one bad phone call away from losing everything.”

After this month’s historic midterm elections in the US, where Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress by wide margins, there will be few areas of agreement with Democrats’ Republican counterparts – and President Donald Trump.

But targeted reforms that address the high cost of prescriptions could be an area where both parties find common ground.

A survey conducted by Fabrizio Ward in March 2025 found more than three in four voters – including 70 percent of Trump supporters – wanted Congress to take action on reducing drug prices.

The issue was the focus of a US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday of last week, when lawmakers and healthcare experts examined how pharmaceutical companies and insurers influence pricing and access to medication.

At that November 17 hearing, witnesses highlighted several factors contributing to high prescription drug costs, including pharmaceutical patent protections and the role of PBMs.

Merith Basey, chief executive officer of Patients For Affordable Drugs Now, argued that pharmaceutical companies exploit the patent system to delay competition from cheaper alternatives.

One of those practices, known as patent thicketing, involves companies securing multiple patents covering different aspects of a medication or its delivery device, potentially making it more difficult for competitors to introduce generic alternatives.

Basey told lawmakers the introduction of generic competition could substantially reduce prices, arguing a single generic competitor can lower a drug’s price by 39 percent, while six or more competitors can reduce prices by as much as 95 percent.

But other witnesses pointed to PBMs, claiming their involvement in distributing drugs can influence pricing.

The Senate panel has advanced a number of proposals to tackle the high cost of prescription drugs in the US. One of those is the bipartisan Eliminating Thickets to Improve Competition (ETHIC) Act, which would limit the practice of patent thickening, making it easier for generic drugs to enter the US market and lower costs.

“Big Pharma knows exactly what it’s doing in monopolising the US patent system: driving up drug costs for Americans while preventing generic-drug manufacturers from getting their foot in the market,” Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, one of the bill’s sponsors, said in a statement.

Wisniewski noted that while the ETHIC Act wouldn’t make her prescription “cheap”, it would be “astronomically better than what we have now”.

news.originalContent:

Iran has flogged a singer and her production team after they were convicted of “offending public decency”, according to local media.

The sentence of 74 lashes handed down to Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her team was carried out in the city of Qom on Monday, the singer’s lawyer Mostafa Nili told the Emtedad news website.

A court in the city had sentenced the quintet in June. They were convicted of “producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online” over a video showing Ahmadi performing without wearing the mandatory hijab alongside male musicians.

The video was posted on YouTube in December 2024. In addition to the flogging, the five were banned for two years from taking part in artistic and musical activities and leaving Iran.

Western governments and human rights groups have condemned flogging as a form of torture that violates international law.

Iran rejects criticism of its human rights record and says Western countries should address abuses of their own.

Iran’s mandatory hijab rules became a focal point of protests in 2022 after Mahsa Amini, a Kurdish Iranian woman, died in custody following her arrest for allegedly violating the dress code.

More women have since defied the rules in Tehran and elsewhere in Iran, while authorities have enforced them more selectively.

news.originalContent:
Questions are being asked about how the big cat arrived, with suspicion falling on the country’s growing role as a hub for wild-animal smuggling.

Police and animal welfare teams have launched a hunt for a lioness reported to be prowling the outskirts of Istanbul.

City authorities closed a woodland area in the northern Sariyer district on Monday as the teams expanded a search for the big cat, which was spotted in the area the previous evening.

Turkiye’s National Parks Directorate said on Sunday that police officers in Zekeriyakoy, north of Istanbul’s European side, had reported spotting “an animal resembling a lion” on surveillance cameras.

Grainy security camera footage republished by Turkish media appeared to show what looked like a big cat prowling across a patch of open countryside.

Istanbul Governor Davut Gul’s office confirmed the information, saying that “the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive”.

The parks authority said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search.

More than 70 personnel, supported by drones, were searching in and around the nearby Belgrade Forest, which covers 54 square kilometres (21 square miles) north of Istanbul.

Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search on Sunday evening.

“I took my car and went out for a drive hoping to see it,” he told Turkiye’s Cumhuriyet newspaper. “While I was driving, it suddenly jumped out in front of me. At first I was scared. After that, I immediately notified the gendarmerie.”

Residents have been warned of the danger, and police were stationed on roads leading into and out of the neighbourhood.

Sariyer District Mayor Mustafa Oktay Aksu noted that the lioness had not harmed chickens she passed at night, indicating she had been hand-reared. However, he warned that she should still be treated as dangerous.

Meanwhile, activists and professors have questioned how the species was brought into Turkiye.

Doganay Tolunay, a professor in the forestry department of Istanbul University-Cerrahpasa, said on X on Monday that questions that need to be asked should include “how a globally threatened species was brought into our country, how it got through customs, why those feeding it have yet to be identified” and “what will happen if the lion is caught”.

Turkiye has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.

In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Sean Gallup/Getty Images)

Members of Congress on both sides of the aisle broke with President Donald Trump over his involvement in getting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reinstated.

Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement Monday just days after his resignation over his affairs with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese asset and former executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed, and another woman who was reportedly his subordinate at Nvidia. Members on both sides of the aisle expressed frustration with Trump over his role in getting Huang reinstated and said his role as CEO could pose national security threats.

House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Brian Mast released a statement Monday about Huang’s upcoming testimony before his committee. He said the alleged affair with a Chinese asset is “extremely concerning” and that the American people deserve answers on the potential national security breaches.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the reinstatement “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.”

“The decision by the NVIDIA board to reinstate Jensen Huang is indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible,” Jeffries said. “Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce. We will not allow America’s national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain.”

My statement on the egregious decision by NVIDIA to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. https://t.co/bf12B6r1z2

Republican Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon said on X that Nvidia should have ignored the administration’s push to reinstate Huang.

“Jensen Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy,” Bacon said. “Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang. Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China. We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible.”

“As Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs, export controls on our most advanced AI chips has been a top priority. Seeing these reports about Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a Chinese intelligence asset and smuggling some of our most advanced chips into China has been extremely concerning. This is something that we’ve been working on for a long time … The American people deserve answers on Mr. Huang’s relationship with this potential Chinese intelligence answers and Nvidia’s role in allowing these actors to smuggle these chips,” Mast said. (RELATED: Jensen Huang Agrees To Testify Before congress Over Relationship With Alleged Chinese Spy)

As Chairman of the @HouseForeignGOP, export controls on our most advanced AI chips has been a top priority. The reports of Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a Chinese intelligence asset and the smuggling of our most advanced technology to China is extremely concerning. The American people deserve answers.

Trump said he personally intervened in talks with Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang. Trump developed a close relationship with Huang throughout his second term over their shared economic and policy interests.

Trump reportedly asked Vice President J.D. Vance to talk to Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to get the CEO reinstated, The New York Times reported. Vance spoke privately with Huang and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances needed that the administration did not believe Huang posed a national security risk. Following the talks, Nvidia told Trump Sunday that they would announce Huang’s reinstatement Monday.

Republican Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts said Huang’s behavior should have barred him from being reinstated.

“Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement,” Ricketts said. “Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”

Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. His own board described his behavior as lacking “candor.” I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement. Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.

Trump traded nearly $98 million in Nvidia shares in more than 100 purchases and sales since the start of his second term, according to CNBC. The tech company became one of Trump’s three largest individual stock holdings by the end of 2025, which was worth between $12.5 million and $58 million.

Jensen Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy. Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang. Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China. We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer accused Trump of putting his own financial interests first. He vowed that Senate Democrats would “wield their full power” to investigate any wrongdoing by Huang or the Trump administration.

“The Trump Administration’s rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act,” Schumer said. “Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat. Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”

Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat. Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain. We’ll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.

Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren called Nvidia’s decision “reckless” and called on Congress to pass export control bills.

“This reckless decision to bring back Jensen Huang does not change the fact that Huang and NVIDIA still owe Congress answers,” Warren said. “The Trump Administration needs to explain what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials to support Huang’s reinstatement. Huang’s return only increases the urgency to pass bipartisan export control bills and make sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk.”

The Trump Administration needs to explain what "input" was given and by which senior officials to support Huang’s reinstatement. Huang’s return only increases the urgency to pass bipartisan export control bills and make sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk.

“You’ve gotta be kidding me,” Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn told MS NOW.

Democratic New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said Huang and Nvidia still had a lot to answer for.

“A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk. Nvidia’s board may answer to shareholders, but Jensen Huang must answer to the American people about his proximity to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative and the whereabouts of billions in advanced AI chips,” Gillibrand said. “Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s directors must testify to Congress publicly and under oath. I will continue to advocate bipartisan legislation to keep America’s most critical technology out of the CCP’s hands.”

“Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang is outrageous. We still don’t know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia’s own board has completed its investigation,” Democratic Illinois Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi said. “Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him.”

Democratic California Rep. Ro Khanna told USA Today during a Nov. 17 interview that Huang should not return to Nvidia. Khanna is slated to become the next chairman of the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

“He should not return to the company. There are serious concerns that I will be raising when he appears on Dec. 1,” Khanna said.

Khanna’s office did not respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.

Huang agreed to testify on Dec. 1 before the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party about his alleged affair with Alice Huang. Her former firm, Megaspeed, bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips. Nvidia formed a committee Tuesday to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls, CBS News reported.

The Senate Banking Committee announced Monday that Huang is scheduled to testify on Dec. 3.

Lawmakers and Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent expressed concern that China was gaining access to the company’s advanced chips, which are critical to developing artificial intelligence (AI) models. The U.S. barred sales of Nvidia’s chips to China over national security concerns.

Trump was reportedly informed of Alice Huang’s ties to China in 2025 but took no action. The Department of Justice (DOJ) overtook the criminal investigation into Megaspeed following an email from Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter to the Commerce Department, The New York Times reported.

news.originalContent:
Since Feb. 28, when U.S.–Israeli strikes killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, the debates surrounding the war and the rhetoric used by its supporters have endlessly shifted. Demands for unconditional surrender and regime change were quickly replaced by a focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the U.S. Navy’s blockade, and economic sanctions, only to boomerang back to all-out war and escalation once June’s Memorandum of Understanding fell apart.

Two of the Republican Party’s biggest hawks, Ben Shapiro and Republican Montana Sen. Tim Sheehy, have once again shifted the Overton Window. Rather than regurgitating the oft-repeated “finish the job” talking point, or calling for just one more swift, decisive bombing campaign that will topple the regime once and for all, both seem increasingly comfortable saying the quiet part out loud: a literal forever war — which critics warned about back in February — is a reasonable option. (RELATED: Hidden Cost Of War That Trickles Down To Your Grocery Bill Set To Explode In 2027)
